items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I am sorry. I could not understand from the question—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The easiest way forward is to ask the member to repeat the
question.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: I am happy to repeat the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Yes please.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Why did she believe it was acceptable to sit on information
relating to her ministerial colleague’s interfer ence in an active crim inal case until June,
which is the date the New Zealand Herald reporter was given by the police for the
release of the Official Information Act information—the day after she was briefed?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Well, first of all, I did not sit on any information. I had no
knowledge that there was an Official Information Act request in. I had no knowledge of
Maurice Williamson’s phone call until 28 April, Monday, when the police
commissioner briefed me. If the member is  asking about the appropriateness of the
police, then that is an operational issue and I trust the police to de al with that in the
manner in which they have operational independence.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I believe that the member may
have misinterpreted my question. My question related to the date that the police gave
her that they would be releasing the information to the New Zealand Herald, which was
2 months after she was briefed about the Official Information Act request.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, the question, as you have  explained it, was the way I
understood it as well. The Minister said she certainly did not sit on any information and
then she went on to say that if the police have indicated anothe r date, that was an
operational matter. The Minister has addressed that question.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Was the Minister informed by the police that they would not
release the information about Maurice Willia mson’s emails until June, which is what
the New Zealand Herald reporter was told?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: In an earlier answer to that member I told her that the police
commissioner informed me they had inform ed the reporter that because the man was
due to appear in court in the following week  they did not intend to release the emails
prior to that court appearance. That is entirely up to the police to decide that.
6 May 2014 Urgent Debates                                17491
Hon Maurice Williamson—Ministerial Resignation

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received letters from Dr Russel Norman, the Hon David
Cunliffe, and the Rt Hon Wi nston Peters seeking to debate under Standing Order 386
the resignation of the Hon Maurice Williamson. Th e letters relate to a particular case of
recent occurrence involving the administrativ e responsibility of the Government. Not
every ministerial resignation will lead to an urgent debate being accepted. However, the
case in question is not related to a policy ma tter that might be debated in the House on
some other occasion; it relates to the admi nistrative responsibility of the Government.
Furthermore, Mr Williamson has not resigned in respect of just a portfolio
responsibility; he has resi gned as a Minister altoge ther. After weighing up the
circumstances very carefully and the public interest in ministerial probity, I have
decided to err on the side of allowing a de bate today. Dr Norman’s  letter was received
first, and I therefore call on him to move th at the House takes note of an urgent matter
of public importance.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: I move, That the House take note of
a matter of urgent public importance . This cuts to the hear t of our democracy—this
issue around Maurice Williamson—and this cuts  to the issue of whether our democracy
is for sale under this Government. But I think that we should start in this case from the
point of view of the victim of domestic violence, because I think that under our system
everybody is deserving of the protection of the law. Regardless of how rich a person is,
regardless of what connections a person may have, and regardless of the wealth of a
person’s abuser, everybody deserves the protec tion of the law in this country. In this
case we had a Minister intervening to protect the abuser, not to protect the victim, and I
think that is what is truly, deeply appalling above everything else in this case. Here was
a victim of domestic violence—the perpet rator in this case has pleaded guilty to
domestic violence—and here we had a Minist er of the Crown intervening in a police
investigation to put pressure on the police not to go ahead with a prosecution for a
domestic violence incident.
Put yourself in the shoes of all the domestic violence victims across New Zealand. It
is a hard thing to complain in a domestic vi olence situation. It is always difficult, it is
always traumatic, and how much harder is it when you have Maurice Williamson
intervening on the side of your abuser in a domestic violence situation? How much
harder is it for a victim of domestic violence  trying to get justice in this country under
this Government when we have a Minister of the Crown interveni ng to try to prevent
the police from going ahead with the prosecuti on of a domestic violence perpetrator?
That is the actual situation we have just experienced in our c ountry. We have gone
through the experience of a National Party Mi nister ringing up the police in a case of
domestic violence and leaning on the police not to go ahead with the prosecution. So,
from the point of view of the victim, which I think should be at th e heart of this whole
debate, everybody deserves equal protection fr om the law, but the National Party does
not seem to believe that any more. It s eems to think that some people—if you are a
domestic violence abuser who has a lot of money—should get special treatment. That is
what happened in this case.
I think it is important to read from the police email a bout National Minister Maurice
Williamson’s conversation with the police about this case of domestic violence.
Maurice Williamson’s mate was a domestic vi olence abuser in this case. According to
the police email, Mr Williamson rang up a senior police member and said that
somebody should review the matter to ensure  the police were on  solid ground, as Mr
Liu is investing a lot of money in New Zealand. Think about that for a second. Think
17492  Urgent Debates 6 May 2014
about what Mr Williamson—a very senior National Party member, a member of the
National Party for decades, a member of this Parliament for decades—was saying.
Think about what it means. He was saying that  this person, Mr Liu,  had to get special
treatment because he was wealthy. Because he  was planning to invest money in New
Zealand, National thinks that he should get special treatment in the criminal justice
system.
This very senior National Party member of  Parliament and Minister was intervening
in a police investigation to put pressure on the police not to go ahead with the
prosecution of a domestic violence abuser, be cause that abuser was investing money in
New Zealand, because he was wealthy. Think about what that means for our justice
system. Think about what that means for a ll the victims of dome stic violence in New
Zealand. Think about what it is like to co mplain about domestic violence and how
difficult it is to go to the pol ice in a case like this. Then, when you are involved in a
police case like this, you have a Minister of  the Crown intervening on the side of your
abuser to try to stop the police proceeding with the prosecution. That is how low
National has now got.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: It is that low. Mr Gerry Brownlee says “Rubbish!”. I am
sorry, Mr Brownlee, but we have the evidence from the police in front of us right here.
The police email says that Mr Maurice W illiamson, a senior Nati onal Minister, rang
them up and said that he wanted to ma ke sure somebody reviewed this matter—a
domestic violence case. Mr Williamson was intervening to say to them that he wanted
them to review the matter to ensure the police were on solid ground as Mr Liu is
investing a lot of money in New Zealand. What he is saying is that the law is not equal.
We are not all equal before the law, because if some of us are we althy, then they get
special treatment according to National. That is what senior Nati onal Minister Maurice
Williamson has just done in our country in the 21st century, this year. Think about that.
So where did the rot begin that we end up at the point where a senior National
Minister thinks that someone should get sp ecial treatment in a domestic violence case
because they are wealthy? How did we end up in  this situation with this Government in
2014? I would argue that the pr oblem is this. National has adopted the culture of the
world of business, where everything is for sa le—and that is fine and how it is meant to
be; the world of business is all about money—and has applied it to the world of
Government and the world of justice. What it has said is that in the justice system you
can buy your way out. If you are accused of being a domestic violence abuser, and you
have got contacts with the Na tional Party and you are planni ng to invest a lot of money
in New Zealand, then you can buy your way out of it. Maybe another donation to the
National Party would fix it for you. You can have a National Minister ring up senior
police on your behalf if you are a domestic violence abuser. You can have a senior
Minister in the National Government ring up the police and lean on them to not proceed
with the investigation.
So what National is saying is that there is the culture of the world of business, and
there is nothing wrong with the culture of the world of business—we need to make
money in the world of business, and that is fine. But when National brings that over to
the world of justice, and says that the richer you are, the mo re justice you will get, that
is wrong. And what National has done is wrong. What Maurice Williamson did was
wrong. Think about it from the point  of view of the victim of domestic violence. For
once, National should look at its  heart and think about  it from the point of view of the
person who has had violence done against them by their partner.
I would also say that National is applying th is idea that money rules all else to the
world of politics. In the world of politics it is supposed to be one person, one vote. We
6 May 2014 Urgent Debates 17493
are all supposed to be treated equally by th e Government of the day. That is regardless
of how wealthy you are, rega rdless of how much money yo u may give to a political
party. We are all supposed to be treated equally in the world of politics and democracy.
That is the idea of democracy. The whole id ea, what our forefathers and foremothers
fought for over centuries, was that we coul d all have one person, one vote, and be
treated equally by the law and by the Govern ment. The whole idea was that we would
not get special treatment just because we were rich, and we would not get special
treatment just because we donated to a political party. This is where National has lost its
way.
Maurice Williamson and the attitude of Maurice Williamson, I think, have come to
represent everything that is wrong in this  current Government. The amazing thing is
listening to him even after he was sacked as a Minister. He wa s defending the position
that you should get special treatment if you ar e planning to invest lots of money in New
Zealand. This reminds me very much of th e Skycity debate. Where did the rot set in?
Let me suggest to you one pl ace where this may have begun , and that was the Skycity
debate. The idea of the Skycity debate was that this Parliament changed the gambling
laws of New Zealand in order to facilita te Skycity. You could argue that it bought the
law—that might be a bit strong. But you coul d certainly argue that National’s position
was that if Skycity was willing to invest a lot of money, it could get the law changed for
it. That is very similar to the position of  Maurice Williamson, whic h is that if you are
investing a lot of money in New Zealand, you should get special treatment from the
justice system, even if you are a domestic violence abuser.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: That is wrong.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: Mr Brownlee says this is wrong. So he is defending
Maurice Williamson. Let us be clear about  what Maurice Willia mson did. He did not
say that everybody—a domestic violence abuser or a victim—should get treated equally
by the law. Maurice Williamson said no. If you  are planning to invest heavily in New
Zealand, you will get special treatment. He said  that their case must be on solid ground,
so, presumably, everyone else’s case does not need to be on solid ground. But if you are
planning to invest lots of money in New Zealand, the poli ce’s case against you should
be on solid ground.
The Green Party does not believe what Maurice Williamson and the National Party
believe. We believe that all people are equal be fore the law. We believe that all people
are equal under our democracy, and we will defend that position. Every time that the
Green Party has proposed more transparency  around donations to political parties, the
National Party has rejected them—every time. It has rejected every attempt to clean up
the system. Simon Power, to give him his due , did have some respect for the idea that
we need more transparency around the system, and some of the changes that he made
around electoral finance were very, very good. Bu t what we are seeing now is that this
Government opposes every attempt to clean up the political system, and the reason it
opposes every attempt to clean up the polit ical system is that it is defending the
indefensible.
Maurice Williamson has become, I think, the most rotten piece of this whole
ideology that the National Party has adopted, which is th at the more money you have,
the more say you should have in Parliament and in the Government and in our
democracy, and if you have enough money, you should get special treatment under the
criminal justice system. That is exactly what Maurice Williamson was saying in his
intervention in this case.
So this is a pretty simple case. I do not  think it is a complicated issue, actually. I
think that it is quite straightforward. I thi nk that it is good that Maurice Williamson has
been sacked, and good on the Prime Minister for doing it, but the Prime Minister needs
17494  Urgent Debates 6 May 2014
to look in the mirror and see where the rot has set in. Where has this culture arisen that
says that the more money you have, the more  influence you have in politics, and the
more say you have in the criminal justice sy stem? That is wrong, and I think that most
New Zealanders will reject what the Government has been doing in this respect. We
need to clean up politics in New Zealand, and we need to remember that the law is here
to protect all New Zealanders, even if they  happen to be the pa rtner of a domestic
violence abuser who gave a lot of money to  the National Party. Even those victims, Mr
Brownlee, deserve our defence as a Parliament, because the law is here to protect all of
us.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member Dr Russel Norman
is usually moderate, if sometimes assertiv e, in his criticisms, but some of those
criticisms, particularly in respect of domestic  violence, were simply objectionable. It is
disgraceful to allege in this Parliament that  any political party sponsors a justice system
where somehow people can buy their way out of justice. It is simply wrong.
He could have made a more reasonable poin t about the judgment of the Minister in
picking up the phone, but he did not. He chose instead to slur, to smear, and to moralise
from the position of someone who says: “Everyone should be treated equally, but I went
off to see Dotcom.”, who could be a critical part of forming a Government that he wants
to be part of. Why did he go off to see Dotcom? He was not visiting my neighbour in
Dipton, who might expect the same treatment from a Labour-Green Government as Kim
Dotcom got. I challenge the member to get up and say that Phillip Mills’ Green growth
agenda will not be adopted in any form by a future Labour-Green Government—that
there will be no subsidy schemes, no incenti ves, and no support—because if it is, it will
look like Phillip Mills has bought the Green Party with his $65,000 donation. So I just
suggest to the member that he get off his high horse—take just a couple of steps back
down off the saddle—before he wades into this kind of fantastical moralising.
Actually, I am going to indicate support for Maurice Williamson as a Minister. As a
Minister, Maurice Williamson was a good Mini ster. I worked with him on a whole
range of issues. Maurice Williamson was the Minister who put together the package for
dealing with leaky homes, showing in the pro cess of that a great deal of understanding
of the human pressures that go with having a leaky home, the technical issues that were
involved, and the patience needed  in trying to square the ci rcle and find some kind of
workable solution.
Maurice’s enthusiasm for technology is, I think, well-known, but it has had a real
impact for New Zealanders. The SmartGate pro cess at the border is largely a product of
his enthusiasm. The roll-out of ultra-fast broadband is in no small part due to his strong
advocacy for it when the National Party was back in Opposition. He has also done a lot
of work over recent years on one of the more difficult aspects of Government, and that
is getting Government agencies to work together. In this case it was the border agencies,
the Ministry for Primary Industries, the Cust oms Service, and the Immigration Service.
They have had to learn how to work t ogether and to also have a wide-ranging
technology upgrade to ensure that New Zeala nd stays suitably connect ed to the rest of
the world. In fact, Maurice has even been able  to make the portfolio of statistics look
exciting through his enthusiasm fo r the integrated data infras tructure, which is going to
make a real difference to many New Zeala nders as the Government becomes more
effective in delivering results through its public services.
But Mr Williamson knows now what we all need to keep in mind—that is, in return
for the privilege and opportunity of being a Minister, we are fully accountable for all the
judgments we make as a Minister. Although day to day those judgments can fall short
of the ideal, and they sometimes do—they sometimes do—there are some judgments we
make that, as the Prime Minister said, go ove r the line. One of those judgments is to
6 May 2014 Urgent Debates 17495
pick up the phone to take a point of view on the work of the police in their prosecutions.
There has been some discussion about the ex tent of interaction of politicians and the
police around investigations, but none of those excuse that particular judgment. It was a
poor judgment, and he has been held to account.
But, of course, if the Leader of the Opposition was held to account, he would not
have his job either. It is interesting to se e today that the Greens are a better organised
Opposition than the Labour Party is, once again. Once more we saw a small sign of why
the Greens are a sharper, bette r, dominating operation. They got their letter in first for a
snap debate, a snap debate that has been known about for what—5 days? 6 days? And in
that time, the Labour Party was too busy messi ng up its variable savings ratio policy to
be bothered or to have the tim e to be able to get the letter in for the snap debate.
[Interruption] Well, there is accountability in the National Party and in the National
Government. The Minister goes over the lin e; the Prime Minister takes action. How
many mistakes can David Cunliffe make befo re he is held account able by the Labour
caucus? Well, we know the answer: he can  make an endless number of mistakes
because by changing the rules he made sure the caucus could not hold him to account.
Let us just look at today’ s little episode. We have asked the Labour Party one
question about its compulsory KiwiSaver polic y: how much will c ontributions have to
go up to make a difference to  interest rates? That matters because putting up
contribution rates cuts the incomes of hundreds of thousands of low-income New
Zealanders. I thought the Labour Party would give us a number, but David Cunliffe
decided one answer was not enough. He tried three.  So he said, first, “I haven’t got that
number on me.” Then he said: “The research has been done. I’ll bring it next time.” And
then he said: “There is no number.” So we  go into an election campaign—I will say
“helpfully”, from our point of view, but probably not so helpfully for accountability
within the Labour Party—where  under its signature policy the leader of the Labour
Party cannot tell New Zealande rs by how much their pay will be cut if they vote for
him.
We have seen the sharp cont rasts in accountability. David Cunliffe keeps his secret
trust donors secret. Here is a question for the Labour front bench: who donated to David
Cunliffe’s secret trust? To use the words of the Deputy Prime Minister of a proposed
Labour-Green Government, who bought David C unliffe, and is he accountable to his
own front bench and his caucus for those donations? Maurice Williamson has been
accountable—he has paid a price; he lost hi s job—for an action he took on behalf of
someone he knew. Will David Cunliffe be held accountable in the same way? I am
waiting for Labour members to get up and explai n to us whether David Cunliffe will be
held accountable in the same way that Ma urice Williamson has been held accountable.
No? Well, it is all about  accountability. How can the Labour caucus hold David
Cunliffe accountable if they do not know who his donors are? We look forward to
hearing about it.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It seems the Minister of
Finance did not want his full allocation of time. That is hardly surprising, because he
did not really defend the Minister who has lost his job, the Hon Maurice Williamson, at
all. In fact, National’s response to this very  serious breach of mini sterial standards has
been to throw mud at the Green Party, to ignore the subs tance of the allegations, and to
fail to excuse, justify, or defend even once the shocking lapse of ministerial standards
that is now endemic in that National Cabine t. Maurice Williamson is just the latest
Minister to be added to Na tional’s roll of dish onour. There is still room for more to
come, and no doubt there will be more. But last week he joined the ranks of Pansy
Wong, Phil Heatley, Nick Smith, Peter Dunne , and John Banks. It is a long list—long
and growing.
17496  Urgent Debates 6 May 2014
Mr Williamson’s resignation and the issues that led to it are very serious matters that
question the independence of the New Zeal and Police and its ability to conduct
investigations without political interference. New Zealan ders must have an assurance
that Ministers in any Government will no t, cannot, and must not use their positions
either to favour some members of the comm unity or to apply pressure to independent
organisations like the Police. New Zealanders are stunned, New Zealanders are shocked,
and New Zealanders are saddened that that could have occurred at all.
The fact that it did occur tells us a lo t about the culture w ithin National and the
disarray that this Government is coming int o. It is the Prime Mini ster, Mr Key, who is
directly and ultimately responsible for th e growing culture of cronyism—cronyism and
arrogance—on the part of this  National Government. These are the lowest ministerial
standards in a generation. It is a culture that says that  the normal rules of conduct no
longer need apply and th at the rules of the Cabinet Manual  have become mere
guidelines.
It is now allowable, for example, for Ministers and their families to financially
benefit from companies that Ministers have assisted in their ministerial capacity,
without a proper declaration of conflict of interest to either  the Prime Minister or the
public. Why is Judith Collins still a Minister? Those companies, like the one
represented by the donor to Mr Williamson, have donated thousands—tens of
thousands—of dollars to the National Party, a nd that is now business as usual. For this
National Government, politics is no longer any kind of calling. It is simply a business—
cash in, cash out. Standards are down and Ministers are hanging on, and the public is
becoming disillusioned that this Governme nt represents any more their hopes and
dreams for a better future.
The Prime Minister has led this culture of cronyism and entitlement not just by
omission but by deliberate ac t himself, like taking $55,000 from the chairman of
Oravida and then telling the public it was a donation to a charity. The National Party
was the charity. He reinstated Peter Dunne to  his ministerial role, despite the almost
certain truth that he leaked a classified Government Communications Security Bureau
report. He relies upon the vote of  John Banks, who is currently on trial for taking large
amounts of money and then covering it up. He ex cused the Minister of Justice, after she
overruled the Prime Minister, for condoning the actions of Minister Williamson
interfering in a police operational inquiry, not to mention the fact that it was a domestic
violence inquiry and that he was a wealthy foreign donor. In any intervention you would
expect the Minister of Justice to be the first to apply the ru le of law and the conventions
of the Cabinet Manual, but she did not. She sought to overrule the Prime Minister. Why
is she still in office?
That same Minister of Justice is a trained lawyer. She is a lawyer who is trained to
manage and identify conflicts of interest, but she could not manage her own, and she
has most recently taken out her frustration through low, personal attacks on individual
members of the press gallery. These are the standards in John Key’ s National Cabinet.
These are the reasons New Zealanders are losing hope and losing  faith that this
Government can represent any more their aspirations for a better life for themselves and
their children in this beautiful country of ours.
It is proper for us to briefly recall the incidents that led to Mr Williamson’s
resignation. He rang the Counties Manukau district commander in January regarding the
investigation of Mr Donghua Liu after his arrest in December 2013 on assault charges
relating to a domestic incident. Mr Williamson told them to “ensure we are on solid
ground as Mr Liu is investing a lot of money in New Zeala nd.” He did not say Mr Liu
was investing a lot of money in the Nationa l Party, but he was doing that as well. And
since when, in this great c ountry of ours, has the amount of money in someone’s bank
6 May 2014 Urgent Debates 17497
account been able to determine their treatment under the law? That is not the New
Zealand that our people want to see. That is not the country we want to build.
Mr Williamson then said that it was not improper because he was not a friend of Liu.
You might say they were just beach bach buddies. That contrasts with Ms Collins, who
was having dinner with friends whom she coul d not talk to but saying that they were
friends after all. Mr Williamson, however, had helped Mr Liu get citizenship after it was
initially declined. He held his citizenship ce remony in his electorate office the next day.
He encouraged him to buy the holiday home ne xt door. He saw the plans for it, and he
worked on it. How close is that to fore ign money? It is way too close for New
Zealanders. To take that and then interfere in a police investigation to try to get the man
off a domestic violence charge—a plague th at affects one-sixth of all women in New
Zealand—it is no wonder that members of  the National Party across the way are
hanging their heads low.
Denis O’Rourke: Disgraceful.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It is disgraceful. It is not the New Zealand that New
Zealanders want to build.
Very, very sadly, this is not the first o ccasion. First, there was Richard Worth. He
resigned in 2009 after being caught out trav elling to India and talking up aviation
training in New Zealand, all the while operating as the director of New Zealand
Aviation Ltd and holding shares and director ships of an Indian trade group—yet more
undisclosed conflicts of interest, yet more cosy relationships with foreign money. It
took a while, but he eventually left. Then Pansy Wong got it wrong in 2010 on yet
another taxpayer-funded trip to China. This time as a private individual she witnessed
her husband’s business deals, signed a c ontract using her ministerial title, and
promoted—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: She was proved right.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: —here is one for Mr Brownlee—her husband’s
hovercraft business and the inte rests of a local Chinese we bsite. She was too close to
foreign money. A culture of cronyism setting in. It all sounds very familiar, does it not,
given Ms Collins’ current troubles?
In March 2010 Phil Heatley was sacked for mu ch less. He lost his position when it
was revealed he had charged Ministerial Services for expenses he was not entitled to. Or
there is Nick Smith, sitting there, who went—only to return—for writ ing a letter of
support for his friend and National Party campaigner Bronwyn Pullar while he was a
Minister, on his ministerial le tterhead. The Prime Minister de scribed that as a lapse of
judgment, but in the light of Ms Collins, one could feel sorry for that Minister, because
he was treated harshly by comparison.
This goes to the culture within National. It is a culture of cronyism, a culture of
arrogance, a culture of entitlement, a culture that the rules that apply to all other New
Zealanders no longer apply to the Government. There is an old rule in politics that when
that rot sets in a Government goes out.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the Rt Hon Winston
Peters.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Thank God for that. Oh, what a
tangled web she did weave when first she did practise to deceive. Maurice Williamson’s
action in contacting the police was a breach of  ministerial rules. There was no grey area
in his actions; it was a blatant breach of how  Ministers must beha ve. Maurice has done
the appropriate thing and resigned. His Prim e Minister has lauded him for doing so and
has lauded himself as Prime Minister for taking that action.
But what about Judith Collins? Where is  the accountability here for cronyism, for
sleazy favouritism, and for corruption? Th e Minister of Justice was asked, you may
17498  Urgent Debates 6 May 2014
recall, some simple questi ons about a company connected  to her family and her
engagement with the company’s business whilst  on a ministerial visit to China. What is
relevant is that connection, because it determines whether there was a serious conflict of
interest in her actions, whether there was a br each of the Cabinet rules, and whether an
allegation of corruption can possibly be ma de. The Minister’s response was to do
everything and anything but te ll the truth. She explained one of her three engagements
with Oravida in China as being a casual meeting on the way to the airport.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: What’s the debate about?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: The debate is about ministerial standards, and
whether someone—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: No it’s not. Read the letter.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I know that the last pers on to understand ministerial
standards is one Gerry Brownl ee, because, as you recall, there was a new casino to be
set up in Christchurch, and th e new directors were going to  be Gerry Brownlee and the
head of the National Party. He got found out fo r that. So the last person to be able to
speak here on a matter of convention would be Gerry Brownlee. Judith Collins said she
was on the way to the airport.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Tell us about the brown paper bag at the fisheries do.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: He is excited now. I have struck a nerve. We have
struck a nerve. Turn the cameras on to him. I want to see how upset he gets when he
hears the truth. Every action she took was to both withhold the truth and divert focus
from the truth. All these ac tions were bound to fail. And do you know what? She began
to regard herself as being above the rules, above the law, and above convention. She
believes she is beyond reproach and beyond accountability. She blames her staff, and
she blames the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Williamson crossed the line, it is
true. Collins crossed the line countless times and she must go.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will use
the member’s full name.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Certainly I will. The Hon Judith Collins crossed the
line countless times and now she thinks that, when all else has failed, she can take leave,
hide from further scrutiny, and have this s candal blow over. What is the taxpayer to
make of that? You have got Maurice Williams on taking the cop, saying that he made a
mistake, and resigning, but not this one. It  seems that when a Minister comes under
pressure, she stops work, takes a rest, and takes a holiday.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. When the Speaker
decides to require Parliament to set aside time for a debate on a matter that is of public
interest and significance, it needs to be on a topic that is very clearly stated in the letter
to the Speaker. There were four letters to day, I understand, and in  each case, it was
sought to debate the circumstances ar ound the resignation of the Hon Maurice
Williamson. What we have at the moment is a speaker who is using this opportunity to
make accusatory statements in a way that is completely unacceptable and
unparliamentary. I would ask you to call him to  speak within the bounds of the debate
that is in front of us. Otherwise we are unreasonably using up time on a day that belongs
to another event and, ultimately, the time of members tomorrow.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: You would have heard the speech given by the Hon
Bill English. You will also know what the co mplaint was that came to the Speaker with
regard to ministerial rules. That is what th e whole issue is about. What we have got is a
very embarrassed person trying to constrain the debate.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I am going to speak in this de bate very shor tly, but I would
ask you to perhaps read to the House the letter that was su pplied to the Speaker, which
led to the debate.
6 May 2014 Urgent Debates 17499

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: This debate is one around a number of topics to do with
accountability and to do with the ministerial resignation. The Hon Bill English delivered
a speech of around 8½ minutes, approximately  6½ minutes of which were about the
Labour Party, about David Cunli ffe, and about issues related to that. This is a robust
debate, but Mr English’s contribution has raised a number of issues. Mr Peters has been
speaking for a few minutes now on topics clos ely related to ministerial behaviour—far
more closely related than most of Bill E nglish’s speech. I would ask for consistency.
Bill English was allowed to complete his speech; Mr Peters should be allowed to
complete his.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Can I just say to members
that in addressing this issue—[Interruption] We have a point of order on the floor. Can I
just say to members that when  addressing this issue, memb ers, when they respond to a
speaker, are generally given 1 or 2 minutes to respond to what the other speaker has
said. This is a debate about the resigna tion of the Hon Mauric e Williamson from his
ministerial portfolios. Members may refer to  other members in passing, but we need to
remember that the reason for this debate is  the resignation of a Minister from his
portfolio. So I just ask the members to rec ognise that when we come to debate this
issue, and recognise also that all members are honourable members.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Maurice Williamson did not engage in a cover-up,
but what we are seeing now is one. The real issue is who caused all this pressure. Of
course, the answer is when a certain Minister set out to deceive. Maurice did not deny it.

items.speaker: He said
items.text: “I made the phone call.” His explan ation fell short and he went. This is how
democracy is destroyed—when instead of settin g standards and principles of acceptable
ministerial behaviour, the Minister and her Prime Minister so demonstrably fail the
rules. They seem to be in another worl d—a different realm from that of Maurice
Williamson. It is a world where standards of  ministerial conduct do not apply to them.
Why has Maurice gone?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Williamson.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Why has the Hon Maur ice Williamson gone? If I
was him, I would be feeling a bit upset, because it seems that there are nakedly different
standards. Why is Judith Collins still a Minister  if there is a consistent set of Cabinet
rules? Is it the National Government’s contempt or disdain for the public? Is it
arrogance of the type you saw in that point  of order by Gerry Brownlee? He thought, as
Rumpole from down in Christchurch, that he  could offer something by way of a moot
point that we should all take seriously. Ther e is no possible justifi cation, Mr Brownlee,
for your colleague to remain a Minister. It is simply an outrage, an insult to the New
Zealand public. It is an affront to democrac y. What is the taxpayer out there to think?
When they are under the stress and pressure of work, do they get a chance to walk off
home, not be accountable, and face no more questions as to how they are going? No,
they do not. They stick it out because that is part of the job, and a ministerial post, paid
for by the taxpayer, demands the same standards.
Who thinks that it is a mere coincidence, first, that following the dinner—this is what
happened. This is new. It is not known by the members over there, because they are so
indolent and lazy. You had the Ministry for Primary Industries recall of 3 August. You
had the 6 August letter from Julia Xu co mplaining about what has happened to the
company Oravida. Then you had the 20 and 23 October engagements, before and after,
by one Judith Collins. Then you had the sanitary certificate secured by her connections
in China for the company. And then guess what  happened. Its sales, which had hit rock
bottom, took off like a rocket. They soared to millions and millions  of dollars, and Mr
Brownlee thinks he can get up and excuse th at. It is a disgrace. We know that the
National Party is cracking behind the scenes. We know that the reason Maurice
17500  Urgent Debates 6 May 2014
Williamson and Judith Collins should be thanked by us is that they have finally
unveiled the real character and sordid nature  of the modern National Party—cronyism,
sleaze, corruption, all sorts of secret funding.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I just say to the
member—

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: Point of order.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I know what the member is
going to say, and I have been thinking about  it myself. I would just like to refer
members to Speaker’s ruling 26/5 in relation to corruption and disloyalty. I want to read
it to the House because I think it is important when we are looking at this debate. “It is
not only the right, but the duty, of a member who can show that there has been anything
in the nature of bribery or corruption on the part of other members to bring that matter
before the House in the proper constitutiona l way, but a member must not make veiled
suggestions during the course of debate.” That was Speaker Statham in 1934, so it goes
back some considerable way. I just want to  again advise members that all members are
honourable and that is it. Refer to each ot her as honourable, despite what we might
think as otherwise. All of us here are aspi rational and we call a member what we would
want for them and us all to become. I caution the House that we tend to see things in the
world as we are, not as it is, and when we  point one finger at someone else, we point
three at ourselves. So I just caution the member . If he can be careful, please, in the way
in which he is addressing the House.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: There is more to come. The reason Judith Collins is
not telling the truth to this House is that the moment she does, she will not just cease to
be a Minister; she will cease to be a member  of Parliament. For somebody who used to
be on the Law Society—a serious administ ering body up there in Auckland, the biggest
group of lawyers in the country and perhaps the most talented—I say that Judith Collins
is withholding the truth and so are her coll eagues, because they know the consequence.
The trouble is that there is, Mr Brownlee, more to come.
Well, I would have to say that the catchcr y of Winston Peters’ political career has
always been: “There is more to come.”

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: And there was.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: And there was—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: What about those Russian subs?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: —but for one of those moments when the propeller hit
the bottom of the Cook Strait, the Russian subs came in, the surveillance device was on
the Mikhail Lermontov , there was not cash in the br own paper bag at the Kermadec
restaurant, and when he said no, he did no t know what he was saying. But there was
always more to come.
I want to begin my comments today by complimenting the work that the Hon
Maurice Williamson has done as a Minister, to  express my regret that he has had to
make the choice to resign, and to further compliment him for recognising that he had
put a foot over the line and that it was the only consequence that could occur as a result
of that. These things are very hard for pe ople’s families, and so I want to acknowledge
his family, his wife and children, who, of c ourse, will be suffering with him as he is
trying to come to terms with  understanding just how he co uld have had that lapse of
judgment that got him into this position. He  is a good man. He has contributed a lot to
New Zealand—his family should know that—and I am sure that he will continue to do
so for some years to come.
This debate is essentially Parliament sett ing aside time to discuss the circumstances
under which Mr Williamson was forced to—well,  not forced to but decided to resign.
6 May 2014 Urgent Debates 17501
Those circumstances have been well canvassed  through all the outlets  in the media that
this country has. The member himself has made  it very clear that he considers that he
made a mistake. He said that he has had a lapse of judgment and that he was in a
position where he could not continue as a Minister. The suggestion that Mr Williamson
was at any time motivated by the particular wealth of an individual is completely
fatuous. It is as fatuous as me saying that  there is a Christchurch multimillionaire who
funds New Zealand First, for example. Ev erybody knows that that is the case, but no
one actually says it, because it is not appropriate to do so.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Mr Brownlee said that
there are certain things you cannot say. That is  a demonstrable lie that he just engaged
in. He knows full well that a party with the highest return rate for the lowest expenditure
is not the beneficiary of one of his filthy mates.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Can I just say to members—
that is not actually a point of order—that this is a robust place.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Let us consider for just a moment some of the
contributions to this debate today, star ting with Russel Norman. Russel Norman seems
to think that somehow the decision by Maur ice Williamson to resign was an indication
that standards were falling inside the minist erial arrangements we have in this country.
Far from it—it was confirmation that those arrangements are, and continue to be,
upheld. The gentleman concerned went on further to suggest that there was almost an
attitude that if you have got a lot of money, you can get fa vours out of the Government.
Well, that is complete and utter nonsen se. The National Party discloses all its
donations—more so, I would suggest, than most other political parties, because we have
nothing particular to hide.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: What about the trusts?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: For example, the member over there is talking about
trusts. Well, let us talk about David Cunliffe’s trust. Let us  talk about Da vid Cunliffe’s
trust and ask why he cannot tell  us who paid into his accoun t. As the Hon Bill English
said, someone has bought David Cunliffe. Ther e is no question about that. What about
the arrangements between the Green Party and Phillip Mills? Phillip Mills is openly
saying he wants a Green agenda for New Z ealand. He wants his own type of Green
growth agenda for New Zealand. He rejects wh at other mainstream parties are doing, so
he is off to put his money into the Green Party. That is policy for cash—nothing short.
Russel Norman—the great and virtuous Ru ssel Norman—walks up to the Dotcom
mansion and tries to do a deal over Dotcom ’s extradition for cash for the Green Party,
but apparently that is not any sort of misleading or inappropriate behaviour.
What about the Electoral Finance Act that the Labour Party rorted upon the people of
New Zealand, supported by the Green Party? And if you want to  start listing off
Ministers who resign, there were 11 of them  under the previous Government. One of
them, interestingly, was the Rt Hon Wins ton Peters. Maurice Williamson has done the
right thing. He is an honourab le man. He does have a po litical future and he has
contributed an enormous amount to New Zealand at this point. He should be
commended for recognising where the line is, and for him to have made that choice is, I
think, commendable.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Many of the facts of the Maurice Williamson
resignation are extraordinarily clear. On 23 January the Hon Maurice Williamson made
a very clear error of judgment not just by having a conversation with the police about an
open criminal case; by just picking up the phone, he clearly breached the Cabinet
Manual. Many here would probably ar gue that he breached a c onvention that applies to
all members of Parliament, but what is absolutely clear is that he did breach the Cabinet
Manual. In doing so, he undermined two very im portant principles that guide us, as
17502  Urgent Debates 6 May 2014
members of Parliament, but also the justi ce system: firstly, the independence of the
police and the importance of constabulary i ndependence; and, sec ondly, the very fine
line we walk in between advocating for constituents but never abusing our position of
power by being seen to influence the justice system.
The Minister of Police also plays a very important role in defending the
independence of the police. You will see that from time to time the Minister states that
she cannot intervene in something because it is  considered to be operational. But let us
look at the role that the Minist er of Police played in this pa rticular case. The call, as I
have said, was made on 23 January. On 4 Ap ril a media outlet put in a request for
information that the police may have had regarding Maurice Williamson’s intervention
in a case involving Mr Liu and before the c ourts. On 14 April the police flagged with
the Minister’s office in a list of Official Information Act re quests that this request had
been made. The Minister has since released th e text of that descri ption in the briefing,
and it does state simply the name of Mr Liu and does no t include the name of Mr
Williamson. The Minister’s office, of course, you would have thought may have asked
questions about the nature of the release, given how highly politicis ed that particular
National Party donor had been in the past , but accepting the office’s word that no
questions were raised, we move to the next part of the time line.
On 28 April, 2 weeks after the police provide d that small descrip tion of the Official
Information Act request, as the Minister has confirmed in the House today, she was
verbally told by the Commissione r of Police, Mike Bush, th at a request from a media
outlet had been made and it involved Maur ice Williamson. Today in the House we
asked some follow-up, and I believe important , questions about that briefing. When the
Minister of Police was briefed by the commissioner, was she told when the public
would know this vital informa tion about her colleague’s inte rference in a police case?
Did she know at what time and at what da te the public would be told? And had the
journalist been informed of this? She told  the House that the information would be
released—if my recollection is right—the following week or thereabouts, when the
court case was due to come up. The court case is on 10 June.
She also claimed in the House today that sh e was told that the journalist has been
informed that the information would be rel eased to them the next week. The journalist
has not been told. The journalist was not to ld until after she was briefed, and the date
given to that journalist was 10 June. My point  is this: the Minister of Police either
misled the House today or th e police misled her. She kn ew there would be several
weeks before the public would know about th is case. And what did she do with that
information? Absolutely nothing. She did not tell the Prime Minister. She did not even
ask for the emails relating to Maurice W illiamson’s case. In fact, Mr Williamson and
the Prime Minister received the email evidence before she did, which was on the
Wednesday. The fact of the matter is this Mi nister of Police did nothing to protect her
police force. She asked no questions. She heard no evil and saw no evil. Thereby, in
doing so, she failed them and failed to protect their constabulary independence in favour
of protecting her own colleague.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The only people in this place
who have not made mistakes are those w ho have actually not done  anything. In this
instance, Maurice Williamson made a mistake,  he took responsibility, and he resigned
as a Minister. The person whom he inappr opriately phoned on behalf of was prosecuted
and convicted by the courts. On both instances, justice has been done.
The member who has just spoken, Jacinda Ar dern, has wanted to talk time lines, and
her leader has wanted to talk about standard s. I am happy to engage in that. From the
time the Prime Minister knew of Mr Williamson’s conduct, it was 36 hours later that Mr
Williamson resigned. I challenge the member to  compare that with the record of the
6 May 2014 Urgent Debates 17503
previous Government in a far more serious  offending. Members will recall Taito Phillip
Field. He did not just break the rules of the Cabinet Manual; he committed a corrupt
criminal offence for which he went to prison. What was the time line on Mr Taito
Phillip Field, I ask Ms Ardern. She is now hanging her head and so she should, because
it was not 36 hours. It was not 36 days. It was actually a whole lot longer than 36
weeks. So I say to members opposite that befo re they get on their high horse and before
they start throwing stones in this glass house,  they should reflect on their own record of
vigorously defending Taito Phill ip Field under indefensible  circumstances for many,
many different months, and contrast that with the way in which the Hon Maurice
Williamson acknowledged that he was at fault, took responsibility, and resigned.
It was with an element of sadness. I th ink Maurice Williamson is a talented person
who has given this Parliament and this country great service, whether it is in
information technology—and I have a particular  interest and I have big boots to fill in
the role that he has been playing around th e regulation of buildi ngs for earthquakes—
and I think we would all acknowledge that his infamous rainbow speech was a positive
contribution to this Parliament. So it is with sadness.
But, equally, though, I say that anybody w ho questions the high standards that the
Prime Minister, John Key, sets for this administration overlooks the record and
overlooks the facts. There was nothing more  ironic, Annette Ki ng, than hearing Mr
Cunliffe lecture us on standards at the same time as he continues to refuse to divulge
who the major donors to his s ecret trust were. He lectures  us on transparency at the
same time.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Who had the dinners at the restaurant, Nick?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Well, my point to Ms King is this. We would not know
whether Mr Cunliffe has dined at a dinner with his major donors,  because he will not
disclose who the donors are. That is a very clear contrast.
We have heard this afternoon in this debate members speak as though it was an
invitation for an orgy of mud-slinging. I just simply say to members of this House, and
particularly members opposite, that I know why they do not want to debate the Budget.
I know why they do not want to debate the state of the economy—the strong job growth
and the increasing economic confidence. I kno w why they do not want to debate with
Judith Collins crime being at its lowest leve l in 30 years. I know why they do not want
to debate with Tony Ryall the state of the health service. I know why they do not want
to debate the improving education standards. It  is because the truth is that when this
Parliament focuses on debating the issues that  matter, there is onl y one choice for New
Zealand on 20 September. Members opposite want to engage in  an orgy of mud-
slinging because that is their only hope. That is their only hope—that they might be able
to drag down this Parliament and drag dow n politics in New Zealand in the hope that
some of the mud might stick and they might be able to crawl th eir way back to the
Treasury benches. I simply say to this H ouse to get a grip. Maurice has acknowledged
responsibility. He has resigned. Let us get on with the issues that matter.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: I have learnt in 3 very short years here that
this is an extremely rough-and- tumble place. It is actual ly quite a sad thing when a
Minister resigns. Maurice Williamson likes the saying that in this place, one day you are
a rooster and the next day you are a feather duster. Sadly, our friend Mr Williamson has
experienced the rough and tumble of this pl ace. I want to say some very kind things
about an individual who I actua lly think has served this c ountry and this Parliament
very well for many, many years. I grew up livin g in the Pakuranga electorate. The first
time I joined a political party, it was in Maurice Williamson’s electorate. When I went
and worked for a member of Parliament, it was in Maurice Williamson’s electorate
office. If there is a model of someone as a local electorate MP who goes above and
17504  Urgent Debates 6 May 2014
beyond every single time for his constituents to  battle on their be half, it is Maurice
Williamson, the member of Parliament for Pakuranga. Sadly, Maurice’s desire to be
helpful, Maurice Williamson’s desire to go above and beyond for individuals, has led
him to go a bit too far in this case, and he is paying a very high price for that mistake.
I just want to reiterate to this House that  Ministers and members of this Parliament
serve extremely hard and serve very well on behalf of their constituents and the people
they serve. We are all huma ns, though, and from time to time we make mistakes. When
we make those mistakes, it is important that  we bear the consequences, and that is
exactly what has happened with Maurice. Th e Prime Minister has acted appropriately,
as a Prime Minister should do, in accepting the resignation of Maurice Williamson, and
Maurice Williamson did the honourable thing in  resigning for the mistake he made. He
is an honourable member.
Some of the things that we  have heard today from me mbers opposite are absolutely
unbelievable. To be lectured by Winston Pete rs about corruption is like being lectured
by a lady of the night about abstinence. It is so hard to believe. I can think of only one
person who had been referred to the Serious Fraud Office for donation issues, and that
is Winston Peters. To have Russel Norman  stand up in this H ouse and talk about
democracy being for sale, knowing that he we nt to Kim Dotcom’s mansion and talked
about intervening in the extradition proce ss should he ever get into Government, is
simply unbelievable. To have him turn up here now and talk about democracy being for
sale, and to have David Cunliffe stand up and talk about donations and talk about rich—

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I listened to the member
opposite making references to Winston Peters being corrupt and I seek your guidance,
Mr Speaker, as to whether they were appropria te in light of the statements that have
been made about references to members be ing honourable, given that , certainly to my
knowledge, the Rt Hon Winston Peters has never faced, let alone been convicted of,
any—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I hear the member, and I think it is probably
pertinent to just reflect on what has been said. I have been liste ning very carefully, and
the member who was on his feet  said, I think, that  the member whom you are referring
to made some accusations of corruption. I was listening, and I think that probably is
correct, and it was pulled up at that stage. I do not think we  should go back to where a
point of order has been ruled on, but the member speaking did not actually accuse the
member whom Richard Prosser is defending. He said that th at member actually made
the accusation, which I believe was correct, but I think we just need to be a bit cautious
about accusations. I think Assistant Speaker  Robertson made a good call and cited the
Speaker’s ruling that was approp riate. The debate has gone pret ty well; let us just keep
it on that level.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Thank you. No, I did not say wh at Mr Prosser thought I was
saying. Perhaps he might like to listen a bit be tter next time. I was referring to the fact
that members opposite like to lecture us abou t issues when they themselves know that
they very much have some issues and skeletons in the closet that they need to answer
for. To hear David Cunliffe talk to us a bout donations not being declared when we all
know very well, he knows very well, and thos e sitting behind him know very well that
he received donations during a leadership el ection that he subsequently was not willing
to declare—it is absolutely unbelievable for him to come here and lecture us.
When we think about those who have donated to political parties, and when we think
about those people who in the past decade or  so have been highlighted as those who
have received favours from political parties, there are no better examples than from the
time when Labour was in office. Think of names like Bill Liu. Think of names like
Taito Phillip Field, who actually was convicted  of a crime in this country. If Labour
6 May 2014 Urgent Debates 17505
Party members really want to get into the subject of donations, then  I suggest they go
back and look through all of their bank accounts in the time when they were in office,
because there were certain Ministers in their Government who knew very well what was
transacted and who knew very well about de cisions that were ta ken. The Labour Party
members should not come to this House and try to appear as holy as they wish to
appear, because they will come a cropper in the future, I am sure.
Ministerial standards in this Govern ment are high. The Prime Minister has
demonstrated that. Maurice Williamson has demonstrated that he is an honourable
individual by bearing the cons equences of his actions. I just  want to put on record once
again that he is a hard-working member of  this Parliament. I have witnessed that
firsthand, as have the people of Pakuranga. His 27 years in this House will go down as
27 years of very hard work on behalf of New Zealanders, and he should be
congratulated on that.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Well, that was
extraordinary, was it not? Jami-Lee Ross finished his speech by congratulating a
Minister who rang the police to intervene in a case of an assault by a man upon a
woman. That is what Jami-Lee Ross has just do ne. That is the standard of the National
Party—to get up in this House and to defe nd a Minister of the Crown for going and
intervening in a case about domestic violen ce. I think that the actions of Maurice
Williamson were disgraceful. Maurice Williamson has been in this House for 27 years,
and he should have known better. What is interesting to me is that regarding the
standards of behaviou r of Ministers in this National Government, John Key likes to
crow and say “I’ve come down hard on this.” That is only when they are caught out. It
is only when they are in a corner and he has to  move. It is not a high standard; it is just
when they have been caught out and then sudde nly he says “Right, le t’s make sure this
doesn’t happen. Let’s try to shut this issu e down.” And consistently over the 6 years of
this Government, that is what has happened.
They are not high ministerial standards. Th ey are not the standards John Key told
New Zealanders they would be getting unde r a National Government. What it describes
is the kind of behaviour of a Government th at thinks it is above the law and that the
rules do not apply to it. The rules that appl y to other New Zealanders do not apply to
them. Maurice Williamson can pick up the phone and call the Counties Manukau
superintendent—an interesting call to make , I might add, given that the Counties
Manukau superintendent actually was not in char ge of the case. So I am not quite sure
why Maurice Williamson rang him. Perhaps it was because Maurice Williamson
thought that that was somebody whom he c ould influence, somebody he could use his
ministerial power on to ask whether they were on solid ground because this person had
given a lot of money to New Zealand.
That is the second thing that marks this Na tional Government out . It thinks it is
above the rules, and it is out to support the wealthy few. How unbelievable that
someone would think that ringing the police to say this person had given a lot of money
means anything at all. What it means is it speaks to the values of the National Party. It
speaks to the values where money talks. This is all about the donations that the National
Party receives from wealthy New Zealande rs. Money talks. If you donate money, you
are in a different category and the rules do not apply to you. So the National Ministers
think they are above the rules and they thi nk that people who have money are above the
rules. They will do anything to look after th e wealthy few in this country, and it is a
disgrace.
It is all about th e donations that the National Pa rty gets. Mr Liu donated $22,000. In
the case of Oravida with Judith Collins,  we now know that the National Party has
received around $85,000 from Oravida over the last few years. The relationships
17506  Urgent Debates 6 May 2014
between the National Party and big business in  this country are way too close. What
New Zealanders want out of a Government, I believe, is that it will treat all citizens
fairly—that it will give everybody a fair go and everybody an  opportunity. But with the
National Party, be it an individual person or  be it a business, it is the money that
matters; it is not the person who matters.
Judith Collins is still a Minister; Maurice Williamson is not. How can that be? Yes,
Maurice Williamson crossed over a line and he  deserved to go and he resigned. Judith
Collins has consistently misled this Parliame nt, misled New Zealanders, and misled the
Prime Minister about her activities in relation to Oravida. That is bad enough. Any other
Minister would go. David Cunliffe mentioned t oday that Nick Smith went as a Minister
over writing a letter of s upport on ministerial letterhe ad for someone he knew,
something he should not have done. Judith Collins, on a taxpayer-funded trip to China,
orchestrated three events for her husband’s company, Oravida. It was a trip about justice
issues. She got rid of a justice event so she could go 30 kilometres away from the
airport to visit the headquarters of that company for a photo opportunity—an
opportunity that official documents show was to increase the profile of that company.
That is a breach straight away of ministerial standards, but in addition to that, as we
have rehearsed many times, she also then or chestrated a dinner where the directors of
Oravida and an unnamed Chinese border official were present.

items.speaker: Let us be clear
items.text: that dinner was a meeting.  It was a meeting that was pre-arranged 5
days before she left New Zealand. It was a meeting that worried and concerned the New
Zealand Ambassador to China and the head of  the North Asia division of the Ministry
of Foreign Affairs and Trade so much that  even after Judith Collins changed it from
being an official dinner to being a private dinner, they still wanted to provide her with a
briefing. Judith Collins gave it away in the House today, did she not? She said that she
told the New Zealand Ambassador the day after the dinner that nothing untoward
occurred. Why would you need to tell the ambassador that nothing untoward occurred at
a private dinner?

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Unless he was concerned.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: The ambassador was concerned that something untoward
was going to occur. No doubt that is in the not es that he provided for her. She felt the
need to say that nothing untoward had o ccurred. Ambassador Carl Worker, in the
information that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade has released, has actually
quite clearly distanced himself from this dinner. So that is a Minister on a taxpayer-
funded trip on justice issues who orchestrated  three events—she also got the directors
invited to another event in Beijing—while she should have been talking about justice
issues. And she remains a Minister but Maur ice Williamson has been sacked. That is
double standards. It is not just low standard s of ministerial behaviour with John Key; it
is now double standards as well.
This Government is accumulating the impression in the minds of many New
Zealanders—and we have all heard it in the last week—t hat it is who you know that
matters with the National Party, it is how mu ch money you have got that matters with
the National Party, and it is whether you have donated to the National Party that will get
you influence, that will get you inside the door . That is an affront to our democracy.
That is against everything that New Zeala nders believe about an  egalitarian society
where everybody gets a fair go. There is no fair go under this National Government.
The way it has gone about its business, be it with Skycity or be it with Rio Tinto or
wherever it is, indicates the kind  of cronyism that it favours. But it is in these personal
actions that we see the true colours of this  National Government—the true colours of a
Government that will always  put money before people, that will always favour the
6 May 2014 Urgent Debates 17507
wealthy few, and where the standards that John Key told us he would apply to his
Ministers have dropped to an all time low.
I want to refer briefly in that context to th e actions of Judith Collins in relation to the
press gallery, because they fit very much within this. Maurice Williamson resigned.
John Key said he should have resigned. Judith Collins was the person left defending
Maurice Williamson the other day, on Sunday. In doing so, she drew into debate a
member of the press gallery and that person’s family. That is one of the lowest things I
have seen a Minister do among many low things in this term of Gove rnment. It is the

Government if you are not one of its friends. It was petty, it was vi ndictive, and it was

The apology that Judith Collins has made wa s for a mistake. This was not a mistake.
It was a deliberate act, consistent with th e way that the National Government is going
about its business: “Let’s take  out people who dissent from us. Let’s change the law so

elected. Let’s change the law so that students and staff aren’t on university councils.
Let’s silence dissent.” It is bullying, it is nasty, it is vindictive, and that is how this

the rules and that has now no standards within its ministerial system. Maurice
Williamson has resigned. That was the right thing to do. Judith Collins should follow.
John Key should face up to the fact that his Government is now representative of the

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: It is on a sad day toda y that I rise to speak
in this debate. It is sad for a couple of r easons, the first being, of course, that Maurice
Williamson—who has, to date, given 27 years of service to the constituents in
Pakuranga—has made a mistake. He has very clearly made a mistake, he very quickly
saw the error of his ways, and he has paid the price for it—a very high price. I am proud
as a member of his caucus and one of his parliamentary colleagues that he took swift
action in acknowledging that.
But what actually makes me more sad is what then happens in this House when a
parliamentary colleague makes a mistake, says  so, cops it on the ch in, and resigns from
being a Minister. But then what do we de scend into in this  House? Led by the
Opposition parties, we then de scend into the gutter. I actually want to reflect on
comments that I will attribute to my colleague  Chris Tremain. He basically said that if
as a team you are unable to score points from your own succe ss, what do you resort to?
You resort to all sorts of tactics where you play the person, not the ball. That is why it is
a sad day for me in the House today, because I do not think that it is ever a good day for
the New Zealand public to see this kind of display, which is playing the person instead
of playing the ball.
I am quite surprised, actually, that it was led by the Greens. From a political
perspective, obviously they got in before Labour did. Labour was too busy sort of trying
to work out its reshuffle and its realignment of players on its team, with Shane Jones
moving on to a better team. Then, of course , Trevor moves up to a better position but
goes back, literally within hours.
I think the most appalling comment that  came through today was the absolutely
revolting and despicable comment from the speaker from the Green Party suggesting
that anyone in this Parlia ment—anyone in this Parliame nt—would not do their utmost
to protect the most vulnerable in our communities. That comment, I think, is an absolute
disgrace. That, more than anything, has sa ddened me today. I think it is upsetting
because, instead, this place descends into very personal attacks.
17508  Urgent Debates 6 May 2014
I could stand here and I could list other Ministers in other Governments who have
made mistakes, wittingly or unwittingly, and wh at has happened to them. But, actually,
the New Zealand public are not interested in that . What they are interested in is the fact
that we had a Minister  who made a mistake, he copped it  on the chin, and he has gone
as a Minister. We have a Prime Minister w ho has very high standards for his Ministers.
I think Nick Smith said that in 36 hours it was dealt with. But, actually, coming back to
this whole point of the fact  that Opposition members are no t able to score points—they
cannot score points in the real game, and the real game is actually focusing on the things
that matter to hard-working New Zealanders, such as the things we are doing with the
Budget next week, the things that we are doing in terms of impr oving access to health
care for hard-working New Zealanders, and for raising achievement in our schools.
But the most significant area in this debate today is in keeping our communities
safer, because the very Minister whom they are gloating about today is the Minister who
got $26 million worth of P off the streets of Ne w Zealand. I think the sort of thing that
New Zealanders judge their Gove rnment on is the results. This side of the House, this
Government, is delivering results.
I will not take much more time, but I do want  to finish on the results that also matter
to hard-working New Zealanders, and they are in the area of the work that this side of
the House has done on protecting very vulnerable victims. It is this side of the House
that put police safety orders in place, wh ich immediately protect women and children
who are under threat from domestic violence. So it is absolutely abhorrent to me to hear
the sorts of comments that came from the Greens this afternoon in this House. I am
enormously proud of the results  that this side of the House has achieved in terms of
lowering crime rates—the lowest rates in 30 ye ars—and in particular the work we have
done on protecting victims, such as victim s’ notification, victim s’ protection, the
victims’ offenders levy, and we have put money into preventing sexual violence. We
have done more than any Government previously has done in the space of domestic
violence.
It is a sad day in this Hous e, but sad for the reasons that  we descend into the gutter
with the Opposition speakers on a day like today, instead of acknowledging the results
and focusing on the results that this Gove rnment has achieved and will continue to
achieve.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I move, That urgency be
accorded the introduction and passing of th e Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill .
The Government has determined, after careful co nsideration, that this bill be progressed
through all stages under urgency to address an  immediate public heal th concern. This
piece of legislation will immediately re move all interim approved psychoactive
products from the market.
It is not so long ago that we passed the Psychoactive Substances  Bill. It passed
through the House with 119 votes supporting it, and I think the general hope from MPs
was that this scourge on our society would be  better contained if we were to have the
legislation that was proposed. Things move on, and I think it is a tribute to the whole
Parliament that in the last few days there has been a considerable amount of work and
effort from all sides of the House to get a bill to the House today that can be once again
broadly supported.
I think the work that the H on Tony Ryall has done on behalf of Peter Dunne in the
last couple of days has got us to a point wher e we can be confident that once this bill is
6 May 2014 Urgency 17509
passed we are as sure as we can be about removing all of this horrible product from the
market. I am sure that there will be opportunitie s in the future for the House to continue
considering this, because there will always be people who want to put these sorts of
substances in the road of those who believe th ey need them as part of their life. With
those few comments I move the motion.
A party vote was called for on the question, That urgency be accorded.

Hon TONY RYALL (Minister of Health)  on behalf of the Associate Minister of

items.speaker: Health
items.text: I move, That the Psychoactive Substances Ame ndment Bill be now read a first
time. At the appropriate time I intend to move  that the bill be set down for second
reading forthwith, without being referred to a select committee. To begin I would like to
thank all parties in the House for their help in bringing us to this point today. I have
appreciated the great cooperati on that all parties have prov ided in discussions around
their positions and their considerations on this bill, and I think that we bring an
amendment bill to the House today that the gr eat majority of the House has indicated its
willingness to support.
The bill does two things. It ends all interim product approvals and interim retail and
wholesale licences, and it prevents informa tion derived from tests on animals being
used to support a product approval application. The remainder of the primary legislation
remains in place, and it remains the most appropriate way of dealing with emerging
psychoactive substances. The bill has a few other features to s upport those two main
aims of removing all products from the mark et forthwith and rest ricting the use of
animal testing. It provides that all products that have interim appr oval will be recalled,
and that those who have had retail or whol esale licences removed must comply with the
recall. The recall order will re quire all licence holders, including those whose licences
are cancelled by this amendment, to te ll the Psychoactive S ubstances Regulatory
Authority what products they have and confirm how they have been disposed of.
The bill clarifies that the Crown is not  liable for any damages or to pay any
compensation as a result of the amendments . We know that some businesses will lose
money as a direct result of these amendments. Our judgment is that the public health
objectives outweigh those losses, and no compensa tion will be paid for that. It clarifies
that the authority must not approve a product unt il regulations are in effect and unless it
is satisfied that the product poses a low risk  of harm. These regulat ions will be in place
in the next few months.
When Parliament enacted the Psychoactive Substances Act last year, 19 votes to one,
the legislation contained tran sitional provisions that allowed some products to stay on
the market. These were products for which no serious adverse reactions had been
reported. If serious adverse effects emerged later, the authority had the power to revoke
approval immediately. It has used that power  to remove 11 products from the market,
17510 Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill 6 May 2014
most recently on Thursday, 1 May. Serious ad verse reactions have been increasingly
reported to the authorities including vomiti ng, seizures, and psychotic episodes. The
problem that has become apparent is that it is often not possible to attribute reactions to
a particular product. People call the poison cen tres or the centre for adverse reactions
monitoring and say they took synthetic cannabis or legal highs. If the authority does not
know what products caused the adverse effect, it cannot use its power s to intervene. So
