items.speaker: Health
items.text: I move, That the Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill be now read a third
time. I would like to thank all members for their contributions to the debate, and
particularly thank all those party representatives who have  worked so constructively
with the Government over the last 48 hours in respect of the bill, such that we have been
able to build a broad consensus across the House on the issues in the bill.
This bill, when it comes into force, will remove from the market all psychoactive
products with interim approval. The police and the Psychoactive Substances Regulatory
Authority have been working closely to pr epare for the change. Starting today, police
and authority enforcement officers have been visiting retail premises to ensure that
affected parties are aware of their obligations. Retailers are being advised that they need
to secure all products and retu rn them to the wholesaler. Wholesalers are being advised
that they will be required to recall all the products from their customers. Manufacturers
17548 Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill 6 May 2014
will be advised that they will need to recall  all products and dispose of them as directed
by the authority. All parties will be advised th at they can be expected to be visited by
the police and the Psychoactive Substances Regulatory Authority enforcement officers,
and that any non-compliance may affect thei r ability to reapply for a licence under the
full regime.
The day this legislation commences there will be active enforcement. At 12.01 a.m.
on Thursday, 8 May the legislation will come into force and makes it clear that no one
may sell, supply, or possess psychoactive substances. Later that day police and
enforcement officers will visit all retailers to ensure that products have been removed
from public view and are being returned to th e wholesaler. As part of the recall notice,
retailers and wholesalers will  be required to maintain re cords of what products are
returned, when they are returned, and which manufacturers they ar e returned to. This
will be matched against information from  manufacturers about what products they
received, from whom, and when.
It is also very important for us to cons ider the people who may be dependent on the
products that this bill removes from the ma rket. The Ministry of Health expects that
some people will experience serious sympto ms from ceasing to use these psychoactive
products, and withdrawal from these products can last for 2 weeks or longer. I explained
to the House during the Committee stage that the Ministry of Health is working very
closely with the sector to monitor these things. I am advised that the addiction treatment
sector believes it can manage this demand w ithin existing resources, but the Ministry of
Health will continue to monitor that very closely.
On what this legislation does, this Parliament is quite clear. We are removing the
interim licences so these products that were  previously enjoying an interim licence will
no longer have a licence, be licensed, and will not be able to be sold, supplied, or
possessed. We are allowing that the individual retailers can maintain their licence for 2
weeks, and the purpose of this is to enable  the authorities to ha ve access to the retail
premises and ask questions and obtain info rmation from the people with their retail
licences.
The Government is indicating that regulations  will be passed in the next few months
on the testing requirements needed to c onsider any new applications under this
legislation. Parliament is being quite explicit in inserting a principle into the legislation
and making it very clear in a provision th at we will not accept any information that
comes from animal testing in support of any application. Parliament is also being clear
that this is notwithstanding new section 12(2), in clause 6, which makes it clear that we
will be prepared to consider animal-testing data from overseas only when that data can
be used to decline an application under this  legislation. Parliament is also being quite
clear that there will be no compensation.
The message from this Parliament is very clear. As of 12.01 a.m.  on Thursday, these
products are no longer legal and it will be an offence to sell, supply, or possess
psychoactive substances. I would like to thank all members for their participation in this
debate, and give them an assurance that th e Ministry of Health will be working very
closely with the regulatory au thority and the police to ensure that the message is out
there: Parliament has changed the rules; those licences are removed.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Labour supports the
Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill be cause it removes the transition provisions
from the Psychoactive Substances Act, which in effect will remove from the market all
the untested drugs that are currently availa ble on the market, and it also removes the
provisions that allow for animal testing of ps ychoactive substances in any tests that are
used to prove that a psychoactive substance is of low or no risk. It improves, but does
not overturn, the original Psychoactive Substances Act.
I want to remind anybody who thinks that passing the Psychoactive Substances Act
was a mistake that before it was passe d, we had no regulation over psychoactive
substances at all. There was an unknown numb er of products out there being sold from
an unknown number of outlets. When the origin al Act was passed, we took control. We
now know how many products are out there for sale, and more have been removed from
the market since the original Act was pa ssed. We now know how many retailers there
are out there. We even know who wants to im port substances so that they can carry out
research on products to perhaps make th em one day become approved products. We
know a lot more about what is  going on in the le gal high industry as  a result of the
passing of the original Act.
However, it was not enough. It did not sa tisfy legitimate concerns about untested
substances being available on the market and being used by people, particularly young
people, without us being fully cognisant of  what both the short-term and long-term
effects of those products are. The decision to leave on the market the products for which
there had been no previous complaints made was made for legitimate reasons by a select
committee, the Health Committee, that was un der pressure to deliv er on a very, very
short deadline to meet the Government’s requirements. Bu t it was, it turns out, the
wrong decision to make.
Overturning that decision has been an amazing demonstration of people power—the
people who have demonstrated in towns and cities around New Zealand, and the people
who have lobbied their MPs. I do not think there is probably a single electorate MP or
list MP in this House who ha s not had a very la rge number of people come and ask that
we improve the legislation. Those people have worked tirelessly to  ensure that their
representatives understand what it is that they want to have done.
I want to particularly acknowledge in  my own community the people on the
Psychoactive Substances Task Force, which is  a self-established group within the city,
and which I have been a member of. It has involved the police, it has involved
concerned parents, and it has involved health  practitioners. It was formed ostensibly to
make submissions to our local council to make sure it made the best use of the
provisions in the Act to apply a local approved products plan. But also, as time went on,
it became a lobbying vehicle. As a member of  it, I found I was spending more of my
time being lobbied by the people in the group th an talking about what we were going to
talk about with the council. That was fair enough—that was fair enough.
I hope that everybody in that group and pe ople around the country know tonight that
the politicians have listened. We have responded, and I th ink we have responded in a
way that does what people wanted us to do, which is to get rid of these untested drugs
without undermining the original intent of th e legislation. That is a position that, it
seems, a number of parties arrived at independently. We could all see that this bill is the
smart way forward, and I do want to acknowle dge the Minister of Health, Tony Ryall,
for his work in ensuring that we did get cross-party consensus on this legislation.
We want to pass this legislation tonight. I find it slightly ironic that we are rushing to
fix up a mistake that was caused by rushing th e original legislati on, but, nevertheless,
the people want these drugs off the market, a nd that is what Parliament wants to do. We
want to do it tonight, so let us get the job done and do what the people want.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to
speak briefly in this third reading of th e Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill.
Undoubtedly, for 20 years or so, successive Governments have been grappling with
how best to minimise harm from psychoactiv e substances and their use, and availability
in New Zealand has burgeoned over the last few decades. This is a very complex area
and, undoubtedly, those who manufacture psyc hoactive substances are continually
trying to invent new substances that detr imentally affect New Zealand families and
young people. In fact, nowhere in the world ar e there clear answers as to how best to
deal with this problem.
However, as Iain Lees-Galloway has said, prior to the Psychoactive Substances Act,
which we are amending, coming in, we did not  have a regulatory re gime, and there is
little doubt in my mind that the Act remain s the best way we know of dealing with
emerging psychoactive substances. This amen dment bill revokes all interim approvals
for psychoactive substances. It has em erged from an outpouring throughout New
Zealand of the concerns of ordinary people about these substances, and the Government
has acted very decisively. Many speakers have  indicated that perh aps there are simple
solutions. They are wrong. Many people have indicated that the science around ensuring
there is minimal risk is easy. They are wrong. It is not easy, nor is the science around
animal testing.
There is no doubt that the National Gove rnment is constantly monitoring world
literature to do everything possi ble to ensure that we exercise best practice in this
country. I do find it absurd that the Green Part y is abstaining, but, ne vertheless, the rest
of Parliament is in agreement that the best thing we can do is send clear messages at this
stage and then progress on and use best practice science and evidence to ensure we do
everything possible to minimise harm and protect the health of New Zealanders.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. Thank
you very much for this opportunity to speak in the third reading of the Psychoactive
Substances Amendment Bill. As a member of the Health Committee, which heard the
primary piece of legislation, I want to reiterate the sentim ents shared across the House
that the context that the country was faci ng was one where these products were out
there. We needed a regime that regulated them, but what we have seen is that regime
fall short of creating the appropriate fram ework for us to determine what safe
substances are. In fact, what we have seen is that the substances that are currently
available have been incredibly detrimen tal to the health and well-being of our
communities right across the country. It was an honest attempt by the select committee
within the context of a bill that needed to be rushed th rough by 1 August, because the
Associate Minister of Health, the Hon Pe ter Dunne, had temporary class drug notices
for 30 substances and 50 products that would have expired.
We had to react and create a regime th at now has enabled us as a society, a
community, to regulate these products, and I guess the next test for the Minister of
Health is, in fact, the development of the psychoactive product approval process. I know
that that consultation proce ss concluded at the end of Ma rch. It is part of a work
programme that could eventually see some  types of products be available for our
communities. It is within that context th at I want to highlight, from the primary
legislation, the local approved products polic y. As a select committee we were really
clear that local communities, local government, should be empowered with tools to then
be able to say where these products should be sold.
I want to congratulate our local govern ment representatives around the country on
passing the ball back to Parliament so that we could create this framework to enable
safe substances to be sold. I want to highlig ht that the ball is in their court about where
those products can be sold, so all of them should continue with th eir consultations, and
6 May 2014 Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill 17551
with their development of these local appr oved products policies in  anticipation that,
eventually, there may be some products that will be available.
I think it is worth highligh ting that, because we were al so really clear through this
process that prohibition was not the answer. I know that my colleague Kevin Hague had
some particular perspectives around that, given that the most damaging drug in our
country is alcohol, and many New Zealanders die through th e consumption of alcohol
coupled with tobacco. As a mature nati on, we had to have, I guess, a grown-up
conversation about where these psychoactive s ubstances fit within the context of us

I am not going to talk for much longer, but  I do want to highlig ht that there have

community. She took it upon herself, with othe r people within that community, to make
a stand.
I want to acknowledge that engagement, becau se I think that what we have seen in
this process is that democracy does work, th at people actually do have power, and that
when they develop a critical mass, they will get reactions from political parties and
people in power. So we do have to commend the Govern ment for doing something. At
the end of the day it does not matter who di d what because we are all here tonight and

Finally, I want to thank a local group called group calle d the Warriors of Change.
They are young people based in Manurewa. On 11 May 2013 they organised a rally. We

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: I want to begin by, as others have done, thanking the
Minister of Health for consulting the Green  Party on his draft bill, the Psychoactive
Substances Amendment Bill, last night. Agai n I record that the Green Party will be
abstaining on this bill. I know that others have  been puzzled by that, but the simple fact
is this. This bill does two things. One of those things we strongly support and the other
we strongly oppose. It leaves us with no other respectable position.
I want to continue from where I left o ff with my second reading speech. In the
second reading I spoke about some of the reasons that lay behind the widespread
community concerns about the availability of these substances and how those were
based on incorrect understandings of the law and of the situation around this wide range
of substances, and my concern about the failu re of the Government to respond to that
misinformation with leadership and proper info rmation. In this speech I want to focus
not so much on that issue as on the response of the Government to the current situation.
This bill reimposes prohibition. The Law Commission, the Minist ry of Health, the
New Zealand Drug Foundation, the vast majority of submitters on the original bill, the
Health Committee, the Minister of Healt h, and this Parliament were all right—
prohibition does not work. It seems bizarre to me that I need to be making the argument
for that case, since so many members of the House in fact made that point and made
17552 Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill 6 May 2014
those arguments in the various debates that we held in the House on the original bill. I
will not quote members tonight. But the fact is that that is the approach that the
Government is now imposing in the interim.
I am just going to run through some of t hose arguments. The thing about prohibition
is that it does not suppress demand. It may reduce it very s lightly, but the fact is that
demand still exists and the market will stil l respond to that demand with supply. In a
couple of months’ time, if the Campbell Live programme takes its camera crews out to
Naenae, maybe from about 10 o’clock at nigh t through to maybe 1 o’clock or 2 o’clock
in the morning, and instead of going to the shop it goes to the alley behind the shop, it is
going to find demand being met by supply.
Prohibition takes supply out of the hands of regulated, controlled retailers and instead
puts that supply into the hands of criminal gangs or other illicit suppliers. Unfortunately,
what that means is that the drug dealer on th e street in the alleyway behind the shop at
Naenae and the drug dealer in the tinny house are not subject to those same controls.
Those people supplying the demand that will not go away as a result of  this bill tonight
will not be checking people for their ID or for proof of ag e. We should expect that
supply to people under age will increase as a resu lt of this bill. Those people will not be
making a distinction between those products th at are low risk and those products that
are high risk.
We should expect that the s upply of products that are hi gh risk will increase as a
result of this bill. Those people, those illicit drug dealers, will, in addition to having a
range of psychoactive substances—those curr ently legal and those currently illegal—
have, in another pocket, other drugs like me thamphetamine. So the product of this bill
will be that the demand, which will not go away as a result of this bill, will also be met
by the increased supply of currently illicit drugs. We are going to be seeing a significant
increase in harm.
As the prohibition on cannabis has proven, demand is not suppressed by prohibition.
Cannabis is absolutely prohibited, and yet most adult New Zealanders have smoked
cannabis. It has not suppressed the demand. Further, this bill, which is going to be
passed tonight—and I respect th e fact that the Green Party speaks in a minority on this
bill—undermines the very Act that it amends, because what will happ en as this bill is
passed is that it will set the platform for illicit chains of supply for psychoactive
substances, and those chains of supply will st ill exist when the bill takes full effect. So
rather than a managed transition in which we move from having a completely
unregulated market through to having a regulat ed market, we do our best in the passage
of this bill to undermine the regime that we are trying to impose.
Others have spoken about the need for treatm ent services to be put in place, because
one of the consequences of this bill fo r any people who do have  some degree of
dependence on any of the substances that curren tly exist is that they will find that they
suddenly have no access to a legal supply of the substance on which they are dependent.
So that is one of the problems around s upply. I welcome Mr Ryall’s comments about
the preparations he has made, but I note that none of that actually increases the supply
of treatment services. None of  that actually deals with th e withdrawal that we fully
anticipate—which Dr Leo Shep has spoken about—with this bill.
There is another matter related to access to treatment services. With the passage of
this bill, those people who wish to access tr eatment services, or who have a need to
access treatment services, will find those treatment services harder to access, and that is
for a couple of reasons. The first is that there will no longer be information at the point
of sale or on the products about how to access treatment services. So that is one of the
reasons. The other reason is th at in order for people to be  able to access treatment
services once this bill is passed, they will need to admit to criminal offending. That will
6 May 2014 Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill 17553
be a significant barrier for many, as it is fo r those who require treatment for dependence
on other currently illicit substances.
Finally, I want to speak a bout stockpiling, and there has been some reference to
stockpiling in this debate tonight. One of the consequences of this bill and of the
Government’s approach to this bill is th at there will be stockpiling—there has already
been stockpiling—and the consequence of th at is twofold. On one hand, it actually
increases the supply of these substances to fuel the illicit trade that we should fully
anticipate will take effect from tomorrow night, and, on the other hand, it also means
that individuals will have much larger quantities of these substances that will become
illicit. That means that they will be more s ubject to crime. Also, that larger supply of
these substances is inherently more da ngerous. So I am very  disappointed that
rationality and evidence-based policy are the casualties of this bill tonight.
I was proud of the quality of the debate, of the maturity of the debate, that we had
around the original bill, the Psychoactive Substa nces Bill, and I think it is unfortunate
that probably most members of this House unde rstand that the bill that we are passing
tonight will make the harm from these substances worse and not better. The Green Party
will be abstaining on this bill.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: On behalf of New Zealand First, I would like
to rise to support the third reading of the Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill. We
are pleased that prompt action has been taken by the Minister of Health, Minister Ryall,
so we would like to commend him for that  action. We are pleased too with the
participation of all parties in this House and th eir desire to ensure that this legislation is
passed as quickly as possible. There has been huge concern in our communities about
psychoactive substances, and there is no simp le solution to the issue of taking these
psychoactive substances. Whether they are le gal or illegal, we are pleased that the
psychoactive substances that are being sold in shops thr oughout New Zealand will not
be available on Thursday.
We are pleased too to support the new tes ting regime regarding animals. We know
that Parliament wanted to reduce the harm  of these psychoactive substances, yet the
bottom line was that the legislation had to be right, and it was difficult to get it right. On
this occasion we did not get it right. We did not do enough, but tonight we have put it
right.
We wanted to reduce the ha rm that these substances were having right around New
Zealand. We have to thank the people who came into our offices with the very sad
stories about their youngsters who had taken these particular substances and who were
continuing to take these substances. We unders tand that the information is not available
as to how many people are going to actually se ek help regarding the substance-taking.
We know it is far harder to get off these chemical highs than it is to get off the natural
products, so we are told. So I was pleased to hear the assurance from the Minister that
there will be resources available for all of those who seek help in this particular
instance.
It is ironic that the profit margin for the product owners, manufacturers, and sellers
of these particular synthetic dr ugs is large. I was interested to read that the annual retail
sales in New Zealand total around $140 millio n, so it is little w onder that the dairy
owners were not happy when the legislation changed.
I must acknowledge the efforts too of Ju lie King, who organise d the recent marches
right throughout New Zealand. It was a credit to her. It is no little thing to do that, so
thank you, Julie.
Tonight in New Zealand First we are very happy to suppor t this bill. These products
will never be safe. We are pleased that th e products are going to be withdrawn from
shops in our communities. There was not anything positive to come from these
synthetic drugs, only misery.
17554 Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill 6 May 2014

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am pleased to take the last call on this
Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill. I just want to acknowledge Minister Ryall
for the work that he has done behind the scen es. This is a very, very difficult piece of
legislation because it is a very, very difficult area of drug law because of the challenges
that these chemicals present, which the dr ug manufacturers and the drug pedlars have
exploited for many years now—since the late 1990s, in fact.
I am a little shocked, but we expect what we expect from the Green Party. To abstain
on something like this because Green Party members have strong views for and strong
views against, when the New Zealand public  are struggling desp erately with this
subject—this whole Parliament has been—shows us really how unprepared that party is
for ever being on the Government benches, because every day a Government deals with
matters that it has to make tough calls on. We cannot please all of the people all of the
time. That party seems to think that if it ca nnot fall on one side or the other, it will just
sit squarely in the middle. Actually, the New Zealand public expect greater of them—

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Split the bill then.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: —and although I have the greatest respect for Kevin Hague, I do not
actually believe he has done his party any service today. Green Party members have
demonstrated why they should never get anywhere near these Government benches. The
public deserve better from them than abst aining on something that is very, very
important.
What this legislation does is it removes the 41 products that we re on the shelves as
part of the transitional regime. With the benefit of 20:20 hindsi ght, one could suggest
that these products would have been harm ful. They are made up of compounds and
chemicals largely unknown to science that re ally serve only one purpose, in my view,
and that is to make the drug pedlars m oney through the misery of addiction. These
substances lock very quickly into the ne urotransmitting parts of the brain and very
quickly cause addiction a nd goodness knows what other ps ychological disorders. So
this legislation gets rid of those 41 products and says that they will also have to prove
that they are of low harm. I have expressed to  this Parliament that low harm means that
they cannot have a possibility of causing a ddiction—which is harmful—so I will be
watching on with interest as to how this issue is traversed.
It also removes the animal testing provision. I have abso lutely no problem with that.
What we are dealing with here is that if we have to raise the bar and say to those people
that the standard for them as a drug manufact urer needs to be higher, because if it is
going to be used by humans we  do not believe that animal s should be subject to that,
well, that is fair enough. Actually, I do not think we should lose too much sleep if the
onus going on drug manufacturers is  that little bit tougher. So  if they n eed to spend
more millions and it takes them longer to be able to get their product to a position where
it is available to go back on the shelves, then  so be it. I actually hope that what this
legislation does is to put out of business drug pedlars, drug ma nufacturers, and those
who would create addictive s ubstances to create misery through addiction in order to
make money.
I want to commend the Minister of Health for what he has done. I want to commend
colleagues across the House for supporting th is legislation. It is a tough piece of
legislation. It is pioneering stuff. Today this  Parliament has sent a very clear message
about accepting the harms that are created by psychoactive substances. Could I ask the
New Zealand public to please also accept that we all have a choice to make when it
comes to ingesting things like these or other substances. The legal st atus of a drug is
never going to alter the chemical nature of that drug and we should all remember that.
I commend this bill. I think it has been n ecessary, but at least we have got on and
done what needs to be done. I commend it to the House.
6 May 2014 Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill 17555
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Psychoactive Substances
Amendment Bill be now read a third time.
Ayes 107
New Zealand National 59; New Zealand Labour 34; New Zealand First 7; M āori
Party 3; ACT New Zealand 1; Mana 1; United Future 1; Independent: Horan.
Abstentions 14
Green Party 14.
Bill read a third time.

Drugs, Control—Animal Testing of Psychoactive Substances 
Hon TREVOR MALLARD (Labour—Hutt South): In order to record the position 
of New Zealanders opposed to making animals suffer to bring recreational drugs to the 
market, I seek leave to table a petition showing the names of more than 43,000 New 
Zealanders opposed to animal testing of so-called synthetic highs. 
Mr SPEAKER: It is an unusual way of doing thi ngs, but leave has been sought to 
table that particular petition. Is there any objection? There is none. It can be so tabled. 
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House. 
AMENDED ANSWERS TO ORAL QUESTIONS 
Question No. 3 to Minister, 17 April 
Hon JUDITH COLLINS (Minister of Justice) : I seek leave to make a personal 
explanation under Standing Order 354 to correct an answer to question No. 3 on 17 
April this year. 
Mr SPEAKER : Leave is sought for that personal explanation. Is there any 
objection? There appears to be none. 
Hon JUDITH COLLINS (Minister of Justice) : In making my answer to question 
No. 3 on 17 April, I said that after the dinner in Beijing on 20 Oc tober 2013, I went to 
bed. When Mr Robertson then asked me whether I had had di scussions with the 
ambassador after the dinner, I said I could not  recall any discussions. I now realise that 
although Mr Robertson’s question referenced the time after the dinne r, he could have 
meant at any time after the dinner, not just  on the evening of the dinner. For the 
avoidance of doubt, I want to clarify to the House that on the day following the dinner, I 
told the ambassador that the dinner was very nice but very short. I also told him that 
nothing had occurred that was untoward or th at he needed to know about. I am drawing 
this to the notice of the House at the earliest opportunity available to me. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Economic Programme—Budget 2014 and Environmental Policy 
1. CLAUDETTE HAUITI (National)  to the Minister of Finance : How will the 
Budget next week help to lock in the benefits of sustainable economic growth to support 
more jobs and higher incomes for New Zealanders? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : The Budget next week will set out 
the next steps in the Government’s progr amme, which will build on the good economic 
momentum that New Zealanders have seen ov er the past year or so. It will show 
growing fiscal surpluses through to 2018, star ting with a small surplus in 2014-15, and 
show debt beginning to decline as a pe rcentage of the economy. Together with 
households and businesses, the Government w ill continue its programme of policy that 
supports the delivery of more jobs and highe r incomes. We are se eing positive results. 
Employment is rising across the board. Wage s on average are increasing ahead of the 
cost of living. Interest rates are near 50-ye ar lows. The current account deficit is less 
than half what it was 6 years ago. Consumer  and business confidence is high. Also, last 
17476 Questions for Oral Answer 6 May 2014 
week we heard that exports in March passe d $5 billion for the first time, and annual 
exports exceeded $50 billion for the first time.  
Claudette Hauiti : How is the higher growth outlook for the economy translating 
into higher wages for New Zealanders? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: Everyone’s situation is different, and there are New Zealand 
families who are finding the economy challenging. But the benefits of a sustainably 
growing economy are tangible. Over the past 2 years the average full-time wage—that 
is, by the measure used to adjust nati onal superannuation every year—has increased 
from $51,700 to $54,700, an in crease of $3,000. Treasury ’s preliminary Budget 
forecasts show that the average wage will rise further to almost $62,300 by 2018, 
another increase of $7,600 over th e next 4 years. The foreca sts also show that around 
170,000 more people will be working by 2018, at the same time as the average wage 
will be running $7,600 higher than today.  
Claudette Hauiti: What other steps will the Government take in the Budget to help 
support sustainable economic growth, more j obs, and higher incomes over the next few 
years? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Two of the risks to the sustained economic recovery would 
be a blowout in Government spending and a runaway housing market. The Government 
is committed to thoughtful, targeted spending, not a large-scale spend-up, which would 
put pressure on interest rates for households and businesses. We will also continue to 
work to increase the supply of land and new housing to the housing market so that it can 
meet the unprecedented demand, particularly from the sharp turn-round in migration 
figures.  
Claudette Hauiti: What measures would erode the good progress made in helping 
wages to increase faster than the cost of living over recent years?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : There are a number of possibl e measures, but I have seen 
one recently that involves cutting take-home pay by 15 percent, forcing New Zealanders 
into a compulsory savings scheme with cont ributions up to 15 percent. I heard a radio 
report yesterday where one person said: “I proba bly have more mortgage debt than I’ve 
got long-term savings, to be honest, so part  of the way we save is to pay down our 
mortgage.” That person was David Cunliffe, but he wants to take that choice away from 
all other Kiwis.  
Hon David Parker : Given that Treasury is forecasting that New Zealand’s current 
account deficit, under his economic settings, will worsen in the coming years, is he 
concerned that his Government is simply repe ating the same mistakes of the last four 
decades, with a worsening external deficit and whistling in the wind as more and more 
money flows into the housing market rather than the productive sector? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : We are certainly keen to avoid the mistakes of the last 
Labour Government, on whose watch the current account deficit doubled from 4 percent 
to 8 percent. In fact, Treasury does regularly forecast the current account deficit to get 
worse, but it keeps getting better, and I am sure the member will be keen to see that laid 
out for him on Budget day. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does the Minister understand that the ongoing damage being 
done to the New Zealand environment under the policies of his Government will 
undermine New Zealand’s economic performance in the long term? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : No, because the statement is incorrect. Under this 
Government, we have introduced regulation of the exclusive economic zone, which did 
not exist before. There was no environmental regulation in our larger economic zone in 
the ocean—one of the largest in the worl d. It is now comprehensively regulated. 
Secondly, through a collaborative process, which a lot of the supporters of the 
member’s party have participated in, through the Land and Water Forum, we are 
6 May 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 17477 
introducing comprehensive regulation of the qua lity of our fresh water. That has never 
been done before. It is designed to ensure we get the right balance between the use of 
our natural resources, our environmental quality, and our economic opportunities. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does the Minister understand that under the water regulations 
promulgated by his Government, New Zeala nd rivers can have 4½ times as much 
nitrogen as the Yangtze River in China, and how does he think that will affect New 
Zealand’s brand being clean and green? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : No, I do not agree with that. There has just been an 
extensive consultation with the public and, prior to that, with all the interest groups that 
wanted to participate, about exactly what the standards of freshwater quality should be. 
Certainly there are some challenges, but there is general agreement on what those 
bottom lines ought to be and what exceptions there could be to them. We hope that the 
member will have the opportunity to support this Government in legislating and 
regulating for the first time ever for a comp rehensive framework for the quality of fresh 
water in every water body in New Zealand. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does the Minister understand that the water regulations his 
Government is proposing would make water so toxic that it would not be safe to swim 
in, and it would be safe only to wade in b ecause it is a wading standard rather than a 
swimming standard, and how well does he think that will go down in our export 
markets for our “100% Pure New Zealand”, “clean, green” brand? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I think the member is trying to  dramatise this issue for his 
own political benefit. The fact is that we are setting up a process that will allow New 
Zealanders, community by community, to grap ple with the hard issues of what the 
quality of their local freshwater supply ought to be. The member’s description of the 
existing or proposed quality is  simply wrong. There has been  plenty of public debate 
about this. There will be pl enty more. In the end, it will be decided community by 
community, consistent with some national bottom lines. 
Ministers—Confidence 
2. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he 
have confidence in all his Ministers? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes, I do. 
Dr Russel Norman: Does he have confidence that all of his Ministers agree with his 
approach to Maurice Williamson—in that Maurice Williamson “crossed a line” by 
calling the police on behalf of Donghua Liu—given that the Minister of  Justice, Judith 
Collins, on the weekend blamed Mr Williamson’s fall not on the actions of Mr 
Williamson but on the media? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: In answer to the first part of  the question, yes, I do. In answer 
to the second part of the question, I think the member has got that incorrect. 
Dr Russel Norman: Why did the Minister of Justic e attack the media and blame the 
media for Mr Williamson’s downfall, when clearly Mr Williamson intervened in a live 
police investigation regarding domestic violen ce issues in order to try to assist Mr 
Donghua Liu and help him avoid prosecution? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I think, as the Minister hersel f has said, due to a series of 
allegations made that she believes are fals e, she overreached. In that regard she has 
apologised because she made a mistake. Bu t, mind you, that member made a mistake 
when he went grovelling up to the Dotcom mansion.  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Rt Hon Winston Peters: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! This is a point of order. It will be heard in silence. 
17478 Questions for Oral Answer 6 May 2014 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Are you going to allow the last part of that prime 
ministerial answer to stand? Can he just keep on doing it at the end of every answer 
today? 
Mr SPEAKER: It was an unhelpful remark from the Prime Minister. The problem is 
that it was at the end of his answer. I could have thought ab out asking him to withdraw 
it. I did not think that was necessary—this is , after all, a debating chamber. But such 
quips from any Minister giving answers do not help the order of the House. 
Dr Russel Norman: Do all his Ministers understand that New Zealand democracy is 
not for sale, given the repeated pattern by his Ministers in acting—[Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The member has a right to  ask his question,  provided it is 
within the Standing Orders. The member can start his question again. 
Dr Russel Norman: Do all his Ministers understand that New Zealand democracy is 
not for sale, in light of the repeated exampl es of his Ministers in tervening on behalf of 
donors to the National Party? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Yes, we do, and I would make  the point that the National 
Party records all of its donati ons and it makes sure that they are in the public domain, 
unlike, say, the Leader of the Opposition, who has got a secret trust that we do not know 
about. 
Justice, Minister—Performance 
3. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Lea der of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: 
Has Hon Judith Collins failed to meet the “high standards” he expects from Ministers; if 
so, how? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : No. Over the almost 6 years Judith Collins 
has been a Minister, she has made a signifi cant contribution to the Government and the 
people of New Zealand and the portfolios that  she has held. The House will be aware 
that in her recent actio ns in respect of Oravida she put  herself in a situation where a 
perception of a conflict of interest has ar isen. The Minister accepts this and she has 
apologised. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Does the Prime Minister remember giving Judith Collins a 
final warning about misleading by omission; if so, on what basis did he give that final 
warning? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : It was in relation to the Oravida situation. I said there was 
other particular information. I have not s een any particular information come out, 
although I am waiting for the secret donors of David Cunliffe to come out. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Does the Prime Minister consider that Judith Collins misled 
the media with her comments about Televisi on One journalist Katie Bradford; if so, 
why is she still a Minister? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : If the member is trying to relate  that to the other issue, as I 
said, that was in relation to Oravida. In re lation to the comments that the Minister made 
about Katie Bradford, she has apologised fo r that. She herself has admitted that she 
overreached. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Was the Prime Minister’s Cabinet Office aware of all the 
Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade advice and briefings  relating to Judith Collins 
and Oravida when it provided him with advice on her conflict of interest? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I am confident that the office is aware of all the pertinent 
information on the advice that it relayed to me. 
Hon David Cunliffe : When, therefore, did he first become aware of the official 
Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade briefings, which said that Judith Collins appeared 
at Oravida in China “To increase the profile  of a successful importe r and distributor of 
6 May 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 17479 
New Zealand products into China.”—i.e., an official function and not a private 
function? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Firstly, I do not have those details with me, but I am happy if 
the member wants to ask me in writing for that. But what is actually quite interesting 
about the documents that the member is readi ng from is, in fact, that laced all the way 
through them—and not only in relation to the very busy schedule that the Minister had 
in relation to the justice portf olio—it was quite clear that th is was a private dinner, and 
that was all the way through the emails, long be fore this issue ever came into the public 
domain. The one thing I do know is that li fting the profile of companies is very 
important. And Shane Jones believes in that; the Labour Party does not. [Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Hon David Cunliffe : Why is the Prime Minister holdi ng this Minister, the Minister 
of Justice and a trained lawyer, to a lower standard than he has held the Hon Maurice 
Williamson, when that Minister, amongst ot her things, has publicly countermanded his 
decision about Mr Williamson? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I am not. I think it will be qui te clear to everyone. In the case 
of Mr Williamson, he breached paragraph 4.14 of the Cabinet Manual.  As I said, in 
relation to Ms Collins, she had a particul ar issue where the accumulation of events 
could have led to a perception of conflict of interest. But let us be honest about this: if 
your making a mistake means you are gone, that leader should have been gone a hell— 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! [ Interruption] When I rise to my feet, the Prime Minister 
should resume his seat. [Interruption] Order! It would be a shame if some Ministers had 
to leave the House so early in this new session. 
Hon David Cunliffe : Why, then, was the Prime Mini ster willing to sack Maurice 
Williamson, Phil Heatley, Peter Dunne, and John Banks, but not Judith Collins? What is 
it about the Minister of Justic e that he will not touch—is it her fund-raising ability or is 
it her influence in the caucus? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : One thing that the member might want to learn if he wants to 
be an efficient leader is th at, actually, every case is c onsidered on a case by case basis. 
This Government has set high standards, a nd, yes, where Ministers have not met the 
standards, they have gone. But, then again, when he does not meet the standards, people 
go as well. It is called Shane Jones. He has gone from Labour— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order!  
Hon David Cunliffe : In light of that answer, can the Prime Minister tell the House 
why he has said that the rules of the Cabinet Manual have now become guidelines? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Well, actually, to be honest, I was paraphrasing Helen Clark.  
Export Sector—Performance and Business Growth Agenda 
4. JONATHAN YOUNG (National—New Plymouth)  to the Minister for 
Economic Development: What recent reports has he received on New Zealand’s export 
performance? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Economic Development) : I have seen the 
recent Statistics New Zealand overseas merchandi se trade report for the first quarter of 
this year. I am pleased to announce to the House that March 2014 was a banner month 
for New Zealand exports. Exports rose by 15 percent compared with March 2013, 
exceeding $5 billion in value for the firs t time. There was a tr ade surplus of $920 
million, the highest ever for a March month. Indeed, in the March quarter there was a 
trade surplus of $1.1 billion—the highest surplus for the series—and it was equating to 
a trade surplus in the last 6 months of almo st $2.5 billion. Our current account deficit is 
now down to 3.4 percent of GDP. In 2008 it av eraged over 8 percent. So the recently 
17480 Questions for Oral Answer 6 May 2014 
rumoured export crisis seems to be about as big a problem  as the much talked about 
manufacturing crisis. 
Jonathan Young: What is the Government doing to  grow new and existing markets 
for New Zealand exporters? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : As part of the Government’s comprehensive Business 
Growth Agenda, we have set an ambitious ta rget of increasing the ratio of exports to 
GDP from 30 percent to 40 pe rcent by 2025. A big part of ach ieving that target is 
developing new and existing international markets for our goods and services. For 
example, trade between New Zealand and Chin a has grown dramatically over the last 5 
years. The Minister of Trade, Tim Groser , has made excellent progress, signing the 
ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement, overseeing the development of 
trade between New Zealand and Chinese Taipei, and advancing negotiations for the 
Trans-Pacific Partnership a nd the comprehensive regional partnership and free-trade 
agreements within the India, Korea, a nd the Gulf Cooperation Council. When you are 
developing exports, there is no  substitute for hard work—a nd it is certainly not fiddling 
around with KiwiSaver when you do not know what you are doing. 
Jonathan Young : What other reports has he s een on New Zealand’s export 
performance?

PSYCHOACTIVE SUBSTANCES AMENDMENT BILL 
First Reading 
Hon TONY RYALL (Minister of Health)  on behalf of the Associate Minister of 
Health: I move, That the Psychoactive Substances Ame ndment Bill be now read a first 
time. At the appropriate time I intend to move  that the bill be set down for second 
reading forthwith, without being referred to a select committee. To begin I would like to 
thank all parties in the House for their help in bringing us to this point today. I have 
appreciated the great cooperati on that all parties have prov ided in discussions around 
their positions and their considerations on this bill, and I think that we bring an 
amendment bill to the House today that the gr eat majority of the House has indicated its 
willingness to support.  
The bill does two things. It ends all interim product approvals and interim retail and 
wholesale licences, and it prevents informa tion derived from tests on animals being 
used to support a product approval application. The remainder of the primary legislation 
remains in place, and it remains the most appropriate way of dealing with emerging 
psychoactive substances. The bill has a few other features to s upport those two main 
aims of removing all products from the mark et forthwith and rest ricting the use of 
animal testing. It provides that all products that have interim appr oval will be recalled, 
and that those who have had retail or whol esale licences removed must comply with the 
recall. The recall order will re quire all licence holders, including those whose licences 
are cancelled by this amendment, to te ll the Psychoactive S ubstances Regulatory 
Authority what products they have and confirm how they have been disposed of.  
The bill clarifies that the Crown is not  liable for any damages or to pay any 
compensation as a result of the amendments . We know that some businesses will lose 
money as a direct result of these amendments. Our judgment is that the public health 
objectives outweigh those losses, and no compensa tion will be paid for that. It clarifies 
that the authority must not approve a product unt il regulations are in effect and unless it 
is satisfied that the product poses a low risk  of harm. These regulat ions will be in place 
in the next few months.  
When Parliament enacted the Psychoactive Substances Act last year, 19 votes to one, 
the legislation contained tran sitional provisions that allowed some products to stay on 
the market. These were products for which no serious adverse reactions had been 
reported. If serious adverse effects emerged later, the authority had the power to revoke 
approval immediately. It has used that power  to remove 11 products from the market, 
17510 Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill 6 May 2014 
 
most recently on Thursday, 1 May. Serious ad verse reactions have been increasingly 
reported to the authorities including vomiti ng, seizures, and psychotic episodes. The 
problem that has become apparent is that it is often not possible to attribute reactions to 
a particular product. People call the poison cen tres or the centre for adverse reactions 
monitoring and say they took synthetic cannabis or legal highs. If the authority does not 
know what products caused the adverse effect, it cannot use its power s to intervene. So 
what we have are products that  have not been tested and that are causing harm, and the 
Government having limited ability to intervene.  
Last month Cabinet discussed this issue, not  for the first time, and agreed that the 
Hon Peter Dunne would arrange for legislatio n to be drafted that would remove all 
products from the market imme diately. It was always inte nded to allow only products 
that had passed rigorous testing and had been shown to pose only a low risk of harm. 
The interim period was intended to last onl y a few months while regulations were 
prepared. However, we still have the products on the market that have not been through 
any testing and it is clearly no longer tenable for this situation to continue, given that the 
serious adverse effects continue to be re ported and that the authority is unable to 
respond quickly.  
On enactment this legislation will revoke  all interim approvals for psychoactive 
products. All products currently on the market will become unapproved products with 
heavy penalties for manufacturing and supplyi ng them. It will also become illegal to 
possess these products, so anyone thinking of stocking up today should bear that in 
mind. This legislation will also cancel all interim retail and w holesale licences and 
begin a recall of all products that had interim approval. Let us be clear here: Parliament 
passes the legislation, the Governor-General signs the legislation, and then at 12.01 a.m. 
on Thursday it becomes illegal to sell, supply, or possess illegal highs, and those 
products must be off the shelves. At 12.01 a. m. on Thursday it becomes illegal to sell, 
supply, or possess illegal highs. The products must be off the shelf.  
The other thing this legislation does is stop tests on animals being used to seek 
approval for psychoactive products. As the Prim e Minister has said, one of the reasons 
why we have had the delay in getting the re gulations prepared is that the Government 
has been reluctant to sanction animal testi ng for these products. I am sure all members 
will be pleased that the bill under consideration will effectively not allow products to be 
tested on animals. The bill prevents the Psychoactive Substances Regulatory Authority 
and the Psychoactive Substances Expert A dvisory Committee from having regard to 
information from animal trials to support the approval of psychoactive products. They 
cannot use any information that has come from  animal testing; therefore, there is no 
reason to do the testing. The only exception is this: the authority may consider 
information undertaken from an  overseas trial if that info rmation indicates that the 
product may not be low risk. So the authority can consider information from an 
overseas trial to protect the heal th of individuals. It cannot c onsider an overseas trial to 
support the approval of a psychoactive substa nce. No one will be doing animal testing 
to support an application here because it will not be able to be used for consideration.  
The rest of the primary legislation remains in place. As we all know, the large 
number of substances and the ability of makers to rapidly change the make-up of 
products mean that traditional approach es do not work. In the long term, the 
Psychoactive Substances Act remains the be st way of dealing with the problem of 
emerging psychoactive substances. I would like to thank all those parties in the House 
who have participated in this process and commend this bill to the House.

The original Ministry of Health standard  for safety—actually, “safety” is not the

Hon TONY RYALL (Minister of Health)  on behalf of the Associate Minister of 
Health: I move, That the Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill be now read a third 
time. I would like to thank all members for their contributions to the debate, and 
particularly thank all those party representatives who have  worked so constructively 
with the Government over the last 48 hours in respect of the bill, such that we have been 
able to build a broad consensus across the House on the issues in the bill.  
This bill, when it comes into force, will remove from the market all psychoactive 
products with interim approval. The police and the Psychoactive Substances Regulatory 
Authority have been working closely to pr epare for the change. Starting today, police 
and authority enforcement officers have been visiting retail premises to ensure that 
affected parties are aware of their obligations. Retailers are being advised that they need 
to secure all products and retu rn them to the wholesaler. Wholesalers are being advised 
that they will be required to recall all the products from their customers. Manufacturers 
17548 Psychoactive Substances Amendment Bill 6 May 2014 
 
will be advised that they will need to recall  all products and dispose of them as directed 
by the authority. All parties will be advised th at they can be expected to be visited by 
the police and the Psychoactive Substances Regulatory Authority enforcement officers, 
and that any non-compliance may affect thei r ability to reapply for a licence under the 
full regime.  
The day this legislation commences there will be active enforcement. At 12.01 a.m. 
on Thursday, 8 May the legislation will come into force and makes it clear that no one 
may sell, supply, or possess psychoactive substances. Later that day police and 
enforcement officers will visit all retailers to ensure that products have been removed 
from public view and are being returned to th e wholesaler. As part of the recall notice, 
retailers and wholesalers will  be required to maintain re cords of what products are 
returned, when they are returned, and which manufacturers they ar e returned to. This 
will be matched against information from  manufacturers about what products they 
received, from whom, and when.  
It is also very important for us to cons ider the people who may be dependent on the 
products that this bill removes from the ma rket. The Ministry of Health expects that 
some people will experience serious sympto ms from ceasing to use these psychoactive 
products, and withdrawal from these products can last for 2 weeks or longer. I explained 
to the House during the Committee stage that the Ministry of Health is working very 
closely with the sector to monitor these things. I am advised that the addiction treatment 
sector believes it can manage this demand w ithin existing resources, but the Ministry of 
Health will continue to monitor that very closely.  
On what this legislation does, this Parliament is quite clear. We are removing the 
interim licences so these products that were  previously enjoying an interim licence will 
no longer have a licence, be licensed, and will not be able to be sold, supplied, or 
possessed. We are allowing that the individual retailers can maintain their licence for 2 
weeks, and the purpose of this is to enable  the authorities to ha ve access to the retail 
premises and ask questions and obtain info rmation from the people with their retail 
licences.  
The Government is indicating that regulations  will be passed in the next few months 
on the testing requirements needed to c onsider any new applications under this 
legislation. Parliament is being quite explicit in inserting a principle into the legislation 
and making it very clear in a provision th at we will not accept any information that 
comes from animal testing in support of any application. Parliament is also being clear 
that this is notwithstanding new section 12(2), in clause 6, which makes it clear that we 
will be prepared to consider animal-testing data from overseas only when that data can 
be used to decline an application under this  legislation. Parliament is also being quite 
clear that there will be no compensation.  
The message from this Parliament is very clear. As of 12.01 a.m.  on Thursday, these 
products are no longer legal and it will be an offence to sell, supply, or possess 
psychoactive substances. I would like to thank all members for their participation in this 
debate, and give them an assurance that th e Ministry of Health will be working very 
closely with the regulatory au thority and the police to ensure that the message is out 
there: Parliament has changed the rules; those licences are removed.

part of the transitional regime. With the benefit of 20:20 hindsi ght, one could suggest 
that these products would have been harm ful. They are made up of compounds and 
chemicals largely unknown to science that re ally serve only one purpose, in my view, 
and that is to make the drug pedlars m oney through the misery of addiction. These 
substances lock very quickly into the ne urotransmitting parts of the brain and very 
quickly cause addiction a nd goodness knows what other ps ychological disorders. So 
this legislation gets rid of those 41 products and says that they will also have to prove 
that they are of low harm. I have expressed to  this Parliament that low harm means that 
they cannot have a possibility of causing a ddiction—which is harmful—so I will be 
watching on with interest as to how this issue is traversed.  
It also removes the animal testing provision. I have abso lutely no problem with that. 
What we are dealing with here is that if we have to raise the bar and say to those people 
that the standard for them as a drug manufact urer needs to be higher, because if it is 
going to be used by humans we  do not believe that animal s should be subject to that, 
well, that is fair enough. Actually, I do not think we should lose too much sleep if the 
onus going on drug manufacturers is  that little bit tougher. So  if they n eed to spend 
more millions and it takes them longer to be able to get their product to a position where 
it is available to go back on the shelves, then  so be it. I actually hope that what this 
legislation does is to put out of business drug pedlars, drug ma nufacturers, and those 
who would create addictive s ubstances to create misery through addiction in order to 
make money.  
I want to commend the Minister of Health for what he has done. I want to commend 
colleagues across the House for supporting th is legislation. It is a tough piece of 
legislation. It is pioneering stuff. Today this  Parliament has sent a very clear message 
about accepting the harms that are created by psychoactive substances. Could I ask the 
New Zealand public to please also accept that we all have a choice to make when it 
comes to ingesting things like these or other substances. The legal st atus of a drug is 
never going to alter the chemical nature of that drug and we should all remember that.  
I commend this bill. I think it has been n ecessary, but at least we have got on and 
done what needs to be done. I commend it to the House.
